subtopic: SUGAR BEET DISEASE-NEMATODE
SUGAR BEET DISEASE-NEMATODE
speechtext:
1.	What areas in Canada are infected with the sugar beet disease known as nematode?
2.	Are any areas infected with any other sugar beet disease? If so, where?
3.	What efforts are being made to control or eliminate these diseases?
4.	Is transport of sugar beets restricted in any of these areas? If so, where, and what transport restrictions or orders are in effect?
5.	Have any representations been made with respect to control or elimination of this disease? If so, by whom ?
6.	Has any provincial government suggested a dominion and provincial proposal, contribution or action to control or eliminate this disease? If so, what provinces made such offer or proposal and what action has the government taken?
7.	What are the main causes for spreading this disease, and what, if any, action by entomologists, engineers or other government agents has been taken or recommended to eliminate such causes?

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: SUGAR BEET DISEASE-NEMATODE
speechtext:
1.	A single field at Glencoe, Middlesex county, Ontario, and twenty-three farms embraced in an area of approximately four square miles at Blackwell, Lambton county, Ontario.
2.	Yes. Sugar beet diseases of at least occasional economic importance in Canada, together with the provinces in which they are known to occur, are listed below:
Cercospora leaf spot (C. beticola)-British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick.
Fusarium root rot of seedlings (F. culrno-rum)-Alberta.
Phoma leaf spot and black leg (Phoma Betae)-British Columbia, Manitoba, Ontario.
Ramularia leaf spot (R. beticola)-British Columbia.
Rust (Uromyces Betae)-British Columbia.
Damping off (Rhizoctonia Solani)-Manitoba.
Black root of seedlings (various fungi)- Ontario.
Black heart (boron deficiency)-Ontario, Quebec.
Curly top (virus)-British Columbia.
Savoy (virus)

Ontario.
Mosaic (virus)-Ontario.
Rhizoctonia rot (Rhizoctonia Solani)- Ontario.
3.	All the diseases listed are under observation or study and where of known value or use recommendations for their control are made known to the affected growers or industries:
Cercospora leaf spot, Fusarium root rot, Phoma leaf spot and damping off are only occasionally sufficiently prevalent to be of economic importance, but not sufficiently so to warrant recommending control measures.
Ramularia leaf spot and rust are occasionally severe enough to cause an appreciable decrease in crops of beet seeds in the Fraser river valley and on Vancouver island, B.C. These are under study at the Dominion Laboratory of Plant Pathology, Saanichton.
Black heart, which occurs occasionally, can be controlled by an application of borax to the soil.
Curly top and mosaic occur occasionally in seed fields, and can be controlled by roguing the infected plants in the seed fields and in the fields where stecklings are being grown.
Savoy is occasionally present in sugar beets destined for the sugar factory. Since infection has already taken place, nothing can be done to control the trouble; removing the infected plants only reduces the crop.	-
Black root of seedlings is prevalent wherever sugar beets are grown in south western Ontario. Several fungi are usually found associated with the trouble, and some adverse soil condition is no doubt partly responsible. It may cause as high as six per cent of the acreage sown to sugar beet in that part of Ontario to be abandoned-ploughed up and sown to something else. It is more prevalent in late sown than in early sown sugar beet fields. This trouble is being investigated by the Dominion Laboratory of Plant Pathology, Harrow.
Rhizoctonia rot of sugar beet may cause a loss of roots as high as 20 per cent in some fields in some years. Crop sanitation and crop rotation are the only practicable means of control.
4.	Yes. The nematode in question, Hetero-dera schachtii, has been designated a plant disease within the meaning of the Plant Disease Act of the Province of Ontario, R.S.O. 1937, chapter 346 (as amended by 1941, chapter 42, and as amended by 1942, chapter 30). The regulations under this act are in force in the Blackwell area described as follows:
"The area in the township of Sarnia, in the county of Lambton, bounded on the north by lake Huron; on the east by the Brigden side-road from lake Huron to the king's highway No. 7; on the south commencing at the Brigden sideroad by the king's highway No. 7 in a westerly direction to where the said highway curves south, thence continuing along the old road which continues westerly from the point
Questions

the king's highway No. 7 curves south to the sideroad between lots 21 and 22; and on the west commencing at the said- old road in a northerly direction to [DOT] lake Huron along the sideroad between lots 21 and 22, and as continued northerly to lake Huron, is hereby designated as a 'precautionary area'."
The transport restrictions in this area, as covered by regulation under this act, are as follows:
"Sugar beets within the precautionary area shall not be transported, except by railway cars, outside of such area and sugar beets from outside such area shall not be transported into the precautionary area provided that sugar beets outside the precautionary area may, with the written approval of the provincial entomologist, be transported to the London Road shipping station.
"(a) Wagons and trucks used in the precautionary area in the handling and delivering of sugar beets shall have boxes with tight fitting bottoms and. tight fitting sides and ends for four inches above the bottoms and shall be free from holes and cracks of sufficient size for dirt to sift through.
"(b) In the precautionary area sugar beets shall be forked from the boxes of the wagons and trucks and all the dirt remaining in the boxes shall in each case be weighed out with the wagons and trucks.
"In the precautionary area dirt shall be returned to the field from which the sugar beets are harvested.
"Earth from railway cars used in the transportation of sugar beets from the precautionary area shall be completely removed by washing at the sugar factory and all such earth and water shall be disposed of in a manner approved by the provincial entomologist."
Further orders in effect are:
"Sugar beets on any field which is found to be infested with the nematode, Heterodera schachtii (Sugar Beet Strain), shall be harvested as early as possible and shipped in as few railway cars as may be arranged.
"Beet seed shall not be grown within the precautionary area.
"If the owner or lessee of any property affected by the provisions of the act or of these regulations, fails to comply with the act or these regulations, or if the owner or lessee of such property is out of the province or his whereabouts are unknown to the inspector, the inspector, with the approval of the provincial entomologist, may make such arrangements as he deems necessary to have such control measures or treatments carried out and any expense incurred shall be payable

by and recoverable from the owner or lessee of any such property in accordance with the provisions of the act."
5.	Yes. By the Canada and Dominion Sugar Company.
6.	No. There being no proposal no action could be taken.
7.	The nematode is spread by flood water, transported in infested soil on the best crop or crop remains, by mud and soil adhering to footwear, the feet of farm animals and equipment. The restrictions stated above in reply to questions 3 and 4 are all designed to reduce to the practical minimum the spread of the nematode. The pest has been under study and investigation since 1931. For the last two years, in cooperation with the sugar company and chemical industry, the dominion Department of Agriculture has been actively studying the utility of soil fumigants as a control measure. These might, if an ideal fumigant could be found, conceivably eliminate the pest.

London, England

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: The house resumed from Wednesday, May 7, consideration of the motion of Hon. Douglas Abbott (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Macdonnell (Muskoka-Ontario), and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Coldwell.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) upon the presentation of his first budget. It might be termed a tax-weary budget, and I predict it will not be his last one.
Before mentioning the various provisions presented to the house, I should like to correct an impression the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) may have made when he answered an interjection of mine in regard to why our young men were leaving for the United States. I suggested the C.C.F.; and the leader of the C.C.F. mentioned that there might be other reasons. To quote him precisely, he said this:
The hon. member asks me about the C.C.F. We were not in power anywhere in Canada from 1930 to 1935 when emigration to the south and deportations to England were on a scale such as we had never had before in the whole period of our history.
That was a Statement which, at that time, I was not able to refute. Since then, however, I have obtained figures

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Order. There is too much noise in the chamber. I must ask hon. gentlemen to moderate their voices, because it is most disagreeable for the hon. member who has the floor.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I have, however, obtained figures for emigration to the United States from Canada for the five-year period ending 1930, and I find that it amounted to 299,000. And for the five-year period ending 1935 it amounted to 37,000, which is in strange contrast with the words of the hon. member, when he said that emigration was on a scale such as we had1 never had before in the whole period of our history.
As to the deportation of people from Great Britain, who had not acquired the five-year citizenship period! in this country, I find that for the whole ten-year period 1932-42 they amounted to 9,501. I should also like to point out that the number of Canadians returning from the United States during the five-year
period ending 1935 was 56,000, whereas the number of Canadians who emigrated to the United States was 37,000. Apparently many Canadians who were in the United States found that conditions in Canada under Right Hon. R. B. Bennett were much more favourable than were conditions in the United States. I trust that the leader of the C.C.F. will be more careful in statements he gives to the house. Up to the present I have always taken them at their full face value; now I realize I must scrutinize every word, and I am afraid I must advise the Canadian public to do likewise.
The Minister of Finance cautioned business not to increase their prices unduly. That was sound advice, and in this regard the minister was following in the footsteps of President Truman. What he said was that business men should reduce their prices as volume and efficiency of business expand. That is all to the good, and a course of action which sound business men willingly follow; for nothing attracts additional competition like high profits.
I should like to put on record the margin of profit on a dollar of sales of some of our representative companies for the year 1946. May I say to the C.C.F. that some businesses did not do so well in 1946 as they did in previous years. I think it will be apparent to the house that the margin of profit per dollar of sales is not as substantial a factor in the price level as is commonly believed, and perhaps the attempt to make business the whipping boy is not as well founded as our C.C.F. friends would like to make out.
The following is a list of companies selected because the figures were readily available, showing the percentage net profit per dollar of sales in 1946: Aluminium Limited, 10-95 per cent; British Columbia Packers, 2-16; Burns & Company Packers, -035, or one-third of one cent; Dominion Dairies, 1-55 per cent; Dominion Stores, 1-29; International Nickel 22-30; Laura Secord candies, 7-91; Loblaw Groceterias, 2-28; Massey-Harris, 3-03; Silverwood Dairies, 1-80; Tamblyn's drug stores, 3-87; Zeller's Limited, 4-36 cents. It is obvious that even in a sellers' market the margin of earnings is a small factor in the price to the consumer.
In relating these percentages to one another two considerations must be borne in mind. One is the rapidity and volume of turnover, and the other is the relative proportion of capital to other factors. If at great capital cost an industry renders itself entirely automatic, as the hydro-electric industry virtually has, almost the sole cost is the servicing of the
The Budget-Mr. Jackman

capital; hence the earnings per dollar of sales must be greater than in many' other industries. This explains why all heavy industries with great plant expenditures must have a relatively high return per dollar of sales. Another factor is that some companies do a single operation and make a profit, while others handle the article from the raw material stage to the consumer's home, and there is only one profit, despite the many handlings.
Earnings generally were good last year due to abnormal volume making up the slack of the war years and the filling of inventory pipe lines and the virtual absence of selling costs. The value which the public is putting on the price of shares would indicate that much harder sledding is ahead.
May I now say a word or two in regard to the figures which the Minister of Finance brought down in his budget. Last year this country contributed to the coffers of the federal treasury almost $3,000 million. The expenditures were $2,632 million, leaving an apparent surplus of $352 million. We may indeed rub our eyes when we see such colossal figures, for it does not seem many years ago when our normal budget of revenue and expenditures ran around $500 million, and the C.N.R. deficits of $50 million were considered by many to be leading the country into bankruptcy. That does seem a long way away from the present. Canada is, however, but the sum total of its people, and no one's individual finances have mounted in anything like the scale in which the dominion government's finances have gone up. Since governments create nothing, the people are therefore entitled to get some idea in regard to taxation and the spending of the huge sums of money which today the government takes from the people.
The government is without question the biggest business in the country, and yet we find in the cabinet thirteen lawyers and two business men. That may be why we have a political rather than a business budget.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A good budget and a good cabinet.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: A people's budget.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We have already heard about the alleged surplus of $352 million arising from the fact that the sales of war assets amounted to $372 million, an extraordinary item. The bonds which were sold to buy these assets are still outstanding and remain unpaid. They are held by the banks, insurance companies and by the people generally, and yet the money which was received

from the sales of these goods was not used to retire any of the debt. Indeed I wonder what the government would 'have done had they received from the sales of war assets not $372 million but let us say $1,000 million or $2,000 million. Surely their consciences would have pricked them then, but the principle remains the same in any situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: We would have reduced the debt by that amount.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Last year there was also the failure to set up an adequate reserve against the large amounts lent to Great Britain and to various European countries for the purpose of rehabilitating them and purchasing goods in Clanada. Altogether about $1,700 million in loans were granted, and yet this government set up a reserve of $25 million. It is very much 'like a good man lending a group of friends, who had been sick or who were recovering from operations about $1,000, hoping that when they recovered they might be able to get on their feet and repay him, but in the meantime he set up a reserve of $15 against 'the possibility that one or more of them would not be able to repay in full. If the government had acted as a business man would naturally act in such circumstances, and set up a reserve of about 20 per cent, the total surplus of $350 million would have been used for that purpose. It serves no useful purpose to fool ourselves about these loans. We hope that they will come back one hundred per cent, but it is only common ordinary prudence to allow for some reserve, and that reserve should be allowed for when the proceeds of these loans are being spent in Canada to swell our whole economy on which our tax rates are based, and on which the coffers of our treasury becomes swollen. This is the time when the reserve should be set up, and not at some other time.
We are not so much interested in the criticism of the government's presentation of its accounts for last year as we are in how it proposes to run the business of the country for the coming year. The estimates last year exceeded expenditures by $137 million. Not only the government but perhaps we of the opposition are also subject to criticism for allowing estimates to go through beyond the spending possibility of the government, and that spending possibility has never been underestimated. Perhaps it might be well if we adopted more of the method carried on in the United States, where appropriations come before the house in a more general over-all way than they do under our system. Certainly when the estimates come down it

The Budget-Mr Jackman
is very difficult to get items substantially reduced, and the government therefore must take the responsibility for the vast expenditures which it has saddled upon the people of the country. This year the estimated expenditures on ordinary account are up $12 million at $1,304 million, or 8108 per head of population. Then we have in addition demobilization and reconversion expenditures of $56 per capita, equal to $164 in all, on both ordinary and special account.
I am quite sure that many people in my riding would rather be content with half the services which the government is providing and have $82 per head returned to them for their own use. Little do they realize that these vast sums of money are being extracted from them, because so much of it is taken silently through indirect taxation. If they could have the money themselves they could spent it in their own way, which they would much prefer to do rather than have the government dictate to them exactly what they shall have and what they shall not have.
I do feel, Mr. Speaker, that the only way we can get our taxation down, the only way in which we can get the economy of this country on a sound basis, is not by attacking all the individual items which come before us in the large blue book of estimates; we must decide how much we can spend, just as any ordinary person or ordinary business would do. Here it has always been the custom to spend all we like on everything we need. Of course, we can afford it because we have twelve million people! But we never seem to think how we shall raise the money or what sacrifices will be entailed on the part of our people when we are considering the spending of money.
We should first of all estimate what we can safely take from the people of Canada in the form of taxation and keep our economy in full production, and then decide how much, and whether all of it would be usefully spent. But as it is, we have gone on spending for years and years various amounts, and the day of reckoning must come when ways and means must be found for the raising of this money. Only last night all hon. members received in their mail an envelope containing a number of blue sheets from the civil service commission advertising for new staff.
I have nothing against any one of these items, which I shall put on the record, but if we do not consider whether we can afford things before we go and spend our money or do our hiring we shall never get the expenditures of the country down and taxes down to a rate where we shall be able to restore incentive to our people. I do not suppose there is a
member in this chamber who could not use the services of some other person. I could use the services of a research worker, as many others no doubt could in their business; we can all use additional staff now and then. If it were merely a question of writing out a ticket and getting additional staff by that simple operation we would have considerable expenses to cope with and there would be nothing left. The cost of services would go up. But this government decides that something may be useful and therefore we must have it.
This is the list of the applications which are called for in the public service. This is in one day's mail. For the experimental farm there are four assistants with salaries from $2,100 to $3,600. Then, also in the Department of Agriculture, there are eight soil specialists, male, with salaries from $2,100 to $3,300. There is an inspector of concentrated milk plants, Department of Agriculture, salary $2,700 to $3,000. In the Department of Mines and Resources they are calling for no less than thirteen associate geologists ranging from $3,000 to $3,900. Then there is a publicity editor and writer for the Department of Fisheries, Ottawa, $3,600 to $3,900. Then we have for the Department of External Affairs, foreign service, officers required, grades 1 and 2, a total of from 25 to 30 with salaries ranging from $2,700 to $3,900.
, I do not doubt for a moment but that all these positions are required or that the persons to be employed would be useful. But this is building up a tremendous overhead for the country to carry, and I do not think we have any proper control. If this goes on we shall get ourselves into the position where the people-those that are left who are not already on the public payroll-will find that they have a crushing burden which they can no longer support, and we shall find ourselves in a first-class depression.
It is only through increased production that we can raise the standard of living. The present budget should be looked at from that point of view and from that point of view alone. Is it a production budget or is it just a political budget? This budget, in the words of the minister, proposes to concentrate the reduction almost entirely in the field of personal income tax. What the minister did was good, but it did not go far enough. He has at last discovered that the people are tax weary, that the present scale, to use his own words again, would constitute a serious impediment to the full working effort and a brake upon the drive and initiative of men and women in all groups and classes-and I would underline "all groups and classes."
The Budget-Mr. Jackman

However else the minister might have liked to distribute his reductions, political and economic necessity required that he should first give attention to the lowering of the personal income tax. This necessity made the budget a comparatively simple one as far as what it did was concerned. Its sins of omission are more important. For those whose modest incomes do not bring them into the taxable brackets, the failure of the government to reduce indirect taxes on a long list of items such as clocks, watches, radios, phonographs, toilet articles, leather goods, telephone and telegraph tolls, silver-plated tableware, candy, soft drinks, to say nothing of the heavy special taxes on amusements, motor cars, tires and the 25 cent tax on a 33 cent packet of cigarettes, the budget brought no relief. These taxes bear most heavily on those who can least afford to pay them. The removal of rent controls and the cancellation of wartime tariff suspensions also increase the cost of living.
Of far greater importance to the low-income group was the withdrawal of subsidies with no compensating benefit. Last year those subsidies which made things seem cheaper than they really were-goods sold below cost- amounted to $208 million, or $17 per head, for every man, woman and child, and when you take the small family budget in the lower income groups, you can realize how much that difference will mean to them.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How much did they save as a result of that?

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The lower income groups?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As a result of the removal of subsidies?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Because of the $208 million. how much was saved to the consumers of Canada?

subtopic: DEBATE ON ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
What I am suggesting is that $208 million was used to subsidize various articles and these subsidies are fast disappearing and the people will have to pay that much more. Perhaps the member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) realizes that butter went up ten cents a pound the next day, and cheese four cents. In my riding, may I say to him, many families will be doubly grateful that this parliament passed unanimously the Family Allowances Act.
What the Progressive Conservative party has advocated for some time would now afford some relief to that great class of taxpayers whose incomes are in the low taxable brackets, and will be hard hit by the increased cost of

living due to the government's action. We have advocated the raising of the minimum exemptions from $750 to $1,000 for single persons and from $1,500 to $2,000 for married persons. The government claims that if the exemptions were increased it would be unfair to those who pay no taxes. What then, may I ask, was the case last year when the very slight increase in the exemptions exempted half a million small taxpayers from paying any tax at all? The government cannot have it both ways. What the government should do is follow a production expansionist policy, and give the workers every encouragement to earn more by producing more. In any event it is not desirable to tax incomes below the $1,000 and $2,000 limits, which I consider "socially necessary exemptions". Our government should not become an agency for lowering the standard of living of the Canadian people.
Let me say here, Mr. Speaker, that experience does not bear out the popularly held opinion, which at one time I shared, that some tax on everyone makes all the people tax conscious and therefore government-spending conscious. The theory seemed good, but the result has been quite to the contrary. The parliamentarian, much less the workingman, can scarcely grasp the billion dollar figures in which we now deal, and the only result of taxation in the brackets below the "socially necessary exemptions", as well as higher rates of taxation above those brackets, has been to demand higher take-home pay. That is the only pay that counts. High taxation- and last year it began at 22 per cent above the minimum exemption of $1.500-was a fruitful cause of labour unrest. Such taxation does not have the educative effect it was believed to have, and results in permanently raising the cost of production.
Apart from the refusal to raise the exemptions, the schedule of reductions is not well designed to raise the standard of living, which can be done only through greater production. The minister used honeyed words when he said:
Nine out of ten taxpayers will find their taxes reduced by 29 per cent or more from existing rates.
That is good politics, because nine out of ten votes are more than sufficient to ensure anyone's election. Perhaps the government forgot to count the very great number who are not taxpayers or who pay very little tax, and to whom the increased cost of living, due to the budget, is worse than a positive increase in taxation. The minister then went on to say:
The reduction as compared with present rates is as much as 54 per cent in the bottom bracket, but is limited to about 6 per cent or 7 per cent in the top brackets.

speakerposition: topic
stagedirection
speechtext:
The Budget-Mr. Jackman
Of course everyone knows that taxation must consider ability to pay-that is, the higher the income the higher the rate-but everyone in all economic classes is faced with greatly increased living costs. The severe impediment to a full working effort, and the brake upon the drive and initiative of men and women in all groups and classes which the minister mentioned, applies to all classes. Extraordinary rates of taxation were cheerfully borne during the war years as a relative small sacrifice; but if the minister had been as much interested in production as in votes, he would have realized that the same carrot which he admitted had to be dangled before the humblest workingman to remove "the serious impediment" or to take "the brake" off, must also be dangled before the biggest business or professional man.
One of the advantages of being a politician is that one has friends in all walks of life; and I have yet to find that people are really very different when it comes to the important things of life. Generally speaking they are moved by the same desires; and two common desires are economic security and advancement, even though they may be on different levels. If the minister felt it was necessary to provide a carrot with 54 per cent nutrition for one class, we might have thought the same reasoning would have led him to follow a similar course, and certainly a course which was better than to have provided a carrot with only 6 per cent nutrition, for those in the upper brackets. The government is budgeting for a surplus next year of $190,000,000, so that there might easily have been a little more nutrition all round and, may I say, a little more production.
A businessman would be just as much interested, if not a little more so, in encouraging those whose work in a competitive market had entitled them to higher pay. Because on them he is relying for his most difficult type of work, and they are the hardest to replace; but not so the Liberal government. Since there are not very many in the higher pay class, their votes are not really important.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Those rates affect the individuals with an income of $250,000. There are not very many of them.
No, and there are not very many above $10,000 a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: They get about twenty per cent.

If the government did what was right, it might be misunderstood politically. A glance at the rapid increase in tax rates, not in the $250,000 bracket with which the Minister of Finance seems to be so familiar-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Just by hearsay.

-but in that bracket after $1,500, we find that on the next $100 the tax is 10 per cent; on the second $100 it is 12 per cent, and it goes up to 18 per cent on the fifth $100 after $1,500. The rate still goes up on a scale which no one could possibly climb, because the degree of ascent is much too great. That shows how quickly the government starts to discourage the worker nowadays. If one looks at the report of the Canadian National Railways and divides the total wage bill by the number of employees, he will find that $2,000 is considerably below the average salary. A married man pays a tax at the rate of 20 per cent on anything over $2,000. Quickly it climbs until at $17,000 it becomes 50 per cent and then climbs up to 80 per cent until it reaches the class with which the Minister of Finance is so familiar.
Then there is the surtax on investment income, which may be substantial. My own opinion is that while there must be some scale, it ascends too rapidly and too high to restore the incentives and to take off the brakes the minister mentioned. Unless some people are human and some are mechanical, I am quite sure that he is wrong.
It is also interesting to look at the comparison of our new rates with those proposed in the United States. Up to $2,750 income the new rates in Canada will actually be lower than they are in the United States. But after $2,750 it will be more expensive to earn your living in Canada than to go across the line. I should have thought that the minister and the government would have been just as much interested in keeping on this side of the line those bright young people, some of our best technically trained young men and women, who are leaving Canada to go to the United States; yet he fixes a limit of $2,750. Let me tell him here and now that that is not the objective which these young people have in mind when they leave our country and go across the border. One wonders why the Minister of Finance, inasmuch as he is an old gunner of the first war, does not raise his sights and aim at the target instead of at no man's land; because that is what he is doing here.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is a striking figure of speech; it is pretty good.

When the minister draws up this scale with the dividing line of $2,750, he is doing something which accomplishes absolutely nothing; because a man earning less than $2,750 is very likely to be a workingman, and let him try to go across the
2S78
The Budget-Mr. Jackman

border. It will be found that he comes under the contract labour classification and is not allowed across the border. But if you take a young man in the white collar class, a university man or other technically trained person, he will have no difficulty in crossing the border. So the minister's proposal accomplishes nothing. He is aiming at a class which cannot get across the border, and he gives no satisfaction to those who can.
Income tax in Canada in pre-war days was sufficiently moderate not to prove a brake on incentive. The rate of increase during the war was astounding; andl in addition to pointing out the need for revenue the government used to argue that because of the increased prosperity and the shortage of civilian goods some of the money or purchasing power had to be drawn off in taxation in order to prevent competitive bidding for goods in short supply. The house will recall that even compulsory savings were resorted to in order to accomplish this end. Many goods no longer are in short supply and it is expected that many producers soon will be looking for buyers. If we are to keep full employment, as much purchasing power as possible should be restored to our people.
One of the greatest disappointments of the whole budget was that it contained no reference at all to the income of married women and the effect that the earning power has on the taxes of the husband. As it stands today a wife may earn only $250; once she earns more than that amount the husband's marital exemption of $750 is reduced dollar for dollar with the wife's income. The result is that if the wife earns $750 or over she is not only taxed by the government but the husband' loses his entire marital exemption of $750. So, looking at it from the standpoint of the family income, the wife who works is subjected to an enormous tax, and this has a very bad effect on our whole working economy. The result is that incentive is gone. What the country needs today in order to meet its problems is more production; but solely as the result of government planning-and I hope my C.C.F. friends will take a look at government planning here-we find married women workers in our light industries, our textile trades, dlress goods factories, domestic help, office help, nurses, and so on, stopping work just as soon as they have earned $250. Yesterday in this very building one of my friends told me his experience was not only that they stopped work; they came to work one day and did not feel like working the next day, when they wanted to go shopping or to do something else. So they just left and did not [ .Mr. Jackman.]
turn up until it pleased them, and did not care very much because they could only work so many days in the year, and if they did not work in his factory there were plenty of other factories looking for work people. So this halter on incentive, if you like, this check on production leads to great difficulties in running our factories, particularly in the light trades. Many of these married women do not have to work; they have available time, and are prepared to work only if there is enough incentive. The previous Minister of Finance said he thought it would be unfair to give the husband his marital exemption in any case, but has the government ever looked into the situation? The fact that a married woman works means that additional family expenses are incurred; there are more meals outside the home,, perhaps someone to do the housework, and less economy in the running of the household. And this whole matter is not one which concerns any real reduction in revenue, because it might easily be shown that there would be a positive increase in revenue if this very foolish taxation of married couples where both are working was removed. So it is simply a matter of government policy, which is foolish in the extreme.
Before leaving the personal income tax brackets might I remind the house that in all the remarks of the Minister of Finance it was implied that such reductions as he brought down were due to the insistent demand of the people, not to government leadership. Further reductions are necessary; but if these incentive reductions must come through popular clamour I fail to see how we are ever going to get a production budget which is so necessary for the welfare of our people, for without business leadership and the ability to assume risk our economy will stagnate and all our people will suffer. At page 2554 of Hansard we find the minister saying:
It is the high marginal rate of tax on additional earnings that discourages additional work, enterprise and initiative, and consequently we must aim in our reductions at cutting down these marginal rates of tax.
Unless some Canadians are human and some are mechanical it is absurd to argue that a man in the 22 per cent bracket, which was the starting bracket after $1,500, needed a reduction to restore his incentive and to take the brake off production, and at the same time to say that the man in the 50 per cent bracket does not need the same treatment. This budget gives one man a 59 per cent reduction and the other a reduction of about 18 per cent.

The Budget-Mr. Isnor
Those who provide business leadership, those who are willing to risk their savings and their capital, are vital to the expansion of our industry and to full employment. Present tax rates prevent saving for investment; they require annual inroads on capital to maintain the standard of living to which their work has entitled them, and result in refusal to undertake the risk of new business because the government shares only the profit and not the loss. They find government bonds, which are as nearly riskless as anything can be, better investments. We need the best brains-
Some lion. MEMBERS: Oh, oh.

-the best management, the best leadership, the best workmen in all fields that we can provide and encourage. I say to some of those who seem to be amused that I certainly do not find the best brains over there.

How is the weather in Halifax?

There evidently is a question about it.
No, not very much.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Not if you go down there.

I should like to touch upon one or two points raised by the hon. member for Rosedale (Mr. Jackman). He referred to the criticism of immigration by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). I do not intend to go into the figures, because it is not necessary; a simple explanation is all that is needed. The same conditions existed in the United States from 1930 to 1935 as unfortunately we had to put up with under the Bennett regime. It is only natural that young Canadians who were in the United States were unable to pay their board and therefore returned home where they would not have expenses to meet. I think to a large extent that is the answer, and it requires no elaboration.
The hon. member referred also to the large revenues we were taking from the people of Canada. The fact that the people of Canada are able to pay that, and pay it cheerfully, indicates the great prosperity we have. I do not think anyone minds paying a fairly good price for an article provided he has the money, but if you have not the money, no matter how cheap a thing is it is still dear. That is an old business maxim that is fairly well recognized. I think we are in a very fortunate position in Canada to be able to carry on in such a cheerful manner.
The hon. member referred to war assets having been taken into consideration in arriving at the surplus. It is true that there was a return of $362 million from the disposal of war assets, but the hon. member must remember that those goods were paid for and charged up in our regular budgets of previous years. You cannot show it in one place and not in another. It was debited to the country in the regular way and naturally when these things are sold the receipts are put into revenues.

This was borrowed
money, and they were paid for out of taxes.

You cannot repudiate a statement made by a former minister of finance that we were both taxing and borrowing to pay for our war effort. It is safe to say that the great bulk of the war assets were paid for out of taxes obtained from the people of this country, so why should not the $362 million go into our revenues?

That is a new way of financing.
The Budget-Mr. Isnor
Does the hon. member know of any better way after we have disposed of the goods than to use the revenue for carrying on our operations? Perhaps at some future time he will enlighten me.
I certainly know a better way, but I do not want to take up your time.

speakerposition: Postmaster General
speechtext: Tell it to the country.

The hon. member referred to this budget as being not a business budget but a political budget. I do not know what he meant by that. It may be because of my lack of experience in the political arena, or because I cannot follow political manoeuvres as well as the hon. member for Rosedale, but I say to him that it does not matter where he goes, he will find people praising the Minister of Finance for one of the finest budgets that has ever been brought down.
Very few.
I am sure it is not the way the hon. member runs his business.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Even in Toronto.
The hon. member for Rosedale says that that is not the way I run my business. I run my business in the same economical manner as the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
And you are equally
successful.
I have the same objective in mindi-not to have a deficit, as happened so often when hon. friends on the other side were in power, but rather to work for a surplus, and a handsome one.
You did not sell part of your building to get a surplus, did you?
You did not charge the cost of your inventory into your sales?

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: I should like to remind hon. members that on second reading of a bill they do not have the right to speak twice.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for trying to prevent these interruptions. However,
I do not mind them because this afternoon we have had it fairly dull up to now. When nine out of ten people you meet are smiling, you know that there is good reason. That reason is to be found in the words used by the Minister of Finance when he said that nine out of every ten are going to enjoy income tax reductions of from 29 to 54 per cent. This budget has been particularly pleasing to a large class of people with which the hon. mem-

ber for Rosedale has not been in particularly close touch, those in the lower brackets who are going to enjoy a 54 per cent reduction.
How much does that 54 per cent work out to in dollars?

I wall tell you in just a minute. To a large number of taxpayers the proposed rates of income tax will bring the Canadian personal income tax below the proposed United States tax. It is true, as the hon. member for Rosedale has said, that there will be a slight difference for those in the higher brackets, but as the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) so rightly said, that is the way it should be. I am for those in that particular income bracket-and perhaps that also will be classed as a political statement. All right; if it is, the fact is that we are looking after the greatest number of our population who are wage earners. Those are the people I am particularly interested in. I know that the hon. member for Rosedale and the people of his particular circle are well able to look after themselves, but I think the government is to be complimented upon taking particular pains to see that the reductions apply particularly to these other people.
Will the hon. member tell me whether I am right or wrong when I say that during the depression years when the Liberal government were in power there were 10,000 people on relief in Rosedale riding?
If there were 10,000 people on relief in Rosedale riding it certainly would surprise me. If that is so, then there was something lacking somewhere in Ontario which I did not know about.
It was under a Liberal government.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
What about your
provincial government?

I can only say that when one is dealing with a budget which applies to all parts of Canada you cannot take one little section of a riding, even though it is considered important by the representative; you must take the over-all picture. At the end of March, 1947, we had the greatest number of usefully and gainfully employed we ever had in the history of Canada, and this is due largely to the policies of the present Liberal government.
WThat about Nova Scotia today?

Yes, what about Nova Scotia?

The Budget-Mr. Isnor
I will answer for Nova Scotia in a moment, but I suggest to the hon. member for Royal that he stick to New Brunswick and let his deskmate ask questions about Nova Scotia.
Don't worry; he can look after himself.

I cannot help thinking back to the evening when the Minister of Finance presented this budget. I sat here looking at the faces of my friends opposite in the Progressive Conservative party. I saw the expressions of wonderment on their faces.
He always was a good performer, with little to work with.

Then I looked beyond, to their left, down to the C.C.F. group. Their faces led me to think that they must be asking themselves: "Could this really happen? Could a budget such as this be brought down, particularly when we have heard so much about blue ruin, depression and the like?" Then I looked into the galleries and I saw there the happy expressions which joined with the Liberals in saying, "Well, that is a wonderful budget."
What were you drinking that night?
In a broadcast I made recently I said I wanted to be fair to the social crediters; they semed to be just as happy as hon. members sitting on the government side of the house.
They do not realize what 54 per cent means.

I remember the generous applause which greeted the Minister of Finance when he rose to speak, and the loud acclaim which was given his opening optimism when he declared, in ringing tones, that the huge and difficult budgets of war years were behind, and that we were all very, very happy to realize that fact. I noted the loud acclaim which met his declaration that Canada is today enjoying matchless prosperity.
May I pause here to pay tribute to a great Nova Scotian, the former minister of finance. I think it is because of his policies, and the policies of the government, that the present Minister of Finance was able to present to the house and the country such a splendid budget.

There must have been some reason.
Mr. ABBOTT [DOT] That is a good one.
I am not detracting at all from the Minister of Finance-and, indeed, he is sincere enough to agree with me on that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And the minister did say it.
In fact I think he is one of the most brilliant men we have ever had in the house.
Which one?
Hear, hear.
What about that fellow who shouts "hear, hear" all the time; what about him?

I was glad to hear the Minister of Finance say that the government was in accord with the general principles of free enterprise, and stated that it was a sensible way of getting things done. I do not wish to discuss this whole question of free enterprise this afternoon, because it might not properly link up with a discussion of the budget-this fine budget which is so acceptable to the people of Canada.
The hon. member for Rosedale referred to increasing supplies. With increasing supplies of materials, with efficiency and cooperation of labour, with greater production and with ample salaries, Canadian business enterprise is in a most favourable position. Last weekend it was my privilege to visit the busy city of Hamilton, and I was pleased with the manner in which they carry on business in that city. Members from all the groups in the house were present, and they, with me, remarked about the efficiency of one plant in particular that we visited, where we saw the complete production from start to finish of a Canadian product. This was not just an assembly plant, but rather a plant doing a complete job. What did the president of that organization say? He said, "We are expanding, and we hope to build another unit"-and he told us the size of it-"which will employ an additional (500, as soon as we can get the materials to build and to go ahead with our plant." There was no blue ruin there, no fear of expanding production so far as that plant was concerned.
The same applies to a great many of our industrial plants. They are not afraid to go ahead because of the excess profits tax, they are expanding as quickly as it is possible for them to do so. This is a good sign for Canada.

The hon. member
missed the best part of the area down there; he went right by it.
The Budget-Mr. Isnor

Oh, no; we saw your part of the country, but like some other sections of Canada you are a little backward so far as the weather is concerned.
Yesterday the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) said there was no relief for business and earlier in the debate the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario could not find anything in the budget that would be good for business. Let me refer to a large class which this budget will affect in a satisfactory manner. I would refer hon. members to the year book for 1945, which shows that in 1941 we had engaged in the wholesale business in Canada 24,758 employers. They, in turn, employed 94,627 males and 22,844 females. In addition there are 13,656 proprietors actively engaged in wholesale lines. I shall add the figures together later on, to show the effectiveness of it.
In the retail business there were 137,331 retail stores employing 297,047 full-time employees. That is subdivided into 188,658 males and 108,389 females. In addition there were 95,561 part-time employees. Added to these were 131,823 proprietor workers engaged in their own stores. These are figures which are worth thinking about. These are the people who are going to enjoy the benefits of the budget in a marked fashion.
In personal services, such as barber shops, beauty shops and the like, there were 14,259. Again referring to the city of Halifax-and possibly I shall be criticized for mentioning this, because of the approaching by-election- we have 915 retail stores, each employing in proportion the same number of employees as are employed elsewhere in Canada. In the town of Dartmouth we have 147 stores. All these will benefit. There is a total of 669,817 taxpayers who will derive direct benefit from the budget.
As at May 1, 1947, the Dominion Bureau of Statistics shows that there were 17,425 reporting employers, who reported 1,853,195 employees. This figure is exceeded only by those of 1943 and 1944. Just think of that- 1,853,195 gainfully employed in Canada at the present time. The average weekly earnings of workers in these firms reporting stood at S35.88 as compared with 832.44 a year ago. A weekly salary of $35.88 for fifty-two weeks of the year would give a total of Sl,850.16 per individual. Of this group of 1,853,195 who averaged $1,850 a year, if single they paid a tax last year of $257. Under the new taxation rates they will pay $180, which means a saving of $77 for each individual, or roughly speaking a saving of 30 per cent of their tax. The married man who was paying $68 will pay

$36 under the new rates, which will give him an additional spending power of $32 or 47 per cent. If you take the number that I have given and multiply it by the $77 saving I have mentioned, you will find that the total saving to this class alone amounts to $142,696,015. That is a remarkable saving, and yet my hon. friends of the opposition rise in their places and say that it does not mean a thing to the average taxpayer.
It does not, if you take the increased cost of living into account.

If you put "ifs" in you can build up any kind of structure. I shall answer by saying if this had not taken place they would have felt the increased cost of living much more.
But speaking of the increased cost of living, I should like to refer my hon. friends to the increases following the first great war as compared with the present situation. I say that is once again a tribute to the present government. They took action which was not taken after the close of the first great war. Because of the control exercised and the foresight of this government our buyers are placed in a splendid position. It is true that the cost of living is high but, to use the word used by my hon. friend, if these controls had not been exercised it would be a great deal higher than it is today.
That will keep them quiet.
It will not keep us quiet because you cannot buy the stuff today. The index is based on the things you cannot get.
The minister from Kings!
Louder.
Knowing that I am a business man I am sure that some of my hon. friends on the other side are wondering what I shall have to say about the excess profits tax.
And the sales tax.

That is about the only thing I have heard any real criticism of over there. They have asked why we did not do away with the excess profits tax to allow expansion of industry in Ontario and Quebec. Even though this may be a little hard for the big men in Ontario and Quebec to take I shall say right here that for the rest of Canada, for the maritimes from which the hon. member for Royal (Mr. Brooks) and the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) come, and elsewhere in Canada with the possible exception of Ontario, it is good news, because they do not want the excess profits tax to be thrown back

The Budget-Mr. Isnor
into the laps of these big men, particularly at the present time when they are still operating to some extent under wartime prosperity. I do not hesitate to say I believe that if we had not put the excess profits tax into effect during the war we would have created a large number of millionaires in Canada, which would not have helped the situation.
Business did not object to it during the war.

What has happened to these men? It is true that they had a standard profit fixed for them on the 1936-39 basis. They were given pretty generous treatment, but they were obliged to pay the excess amount over their normal business, and rightly so. I say that as a business man. Why? Because I believe that owing to the excess profits tax they were able to set up a reserve which it is doubtful that any except a very few would have done. They have that 20 per cent refund coming to them, which is a good nest-egg.
What is the situation if they had a small profit in those years?
In which years?
In the years of standard profit.

The hon. member intimated a moment ago that perhaps he was better versed in business matters than I am. Surely he must know that these men had an opportunity to overcome that difficulty. If they had a depressed business during the period, they were permitted to appear before a board of referees and have a standard profit set. It could have been properly adjusted. In fact during the past two or three months auditors and chartered accountants throughout the country have been kept exceptionally busy because they felt that the excess profits tax would be wiped out and they would not have the opportunity in the future of presenting their case.
Some of them are not adjusted yet.
Some of which?
Some of the standard rates.

There may be the odd one, but the great majority are adjusted. They have cleaned up practically all of them. I would say they have done an exceptionally good job so far as the adjusting of profits standards are concerned.
Were any millionaires mad* in this war?
None of my friends were in that class; therefore I cannot answer.
You did very well.
I was fairly successful; I worked hard. I did not kick about the excess profits tax.
You are saying other people did, which is not correct.

I used it to good advantage, to continue people in employment, to do my little bit toward helping the country.
Since I have paid so many compliments to the Minister of Finance perhaps I may be permitted !to be a little critical at the moment.
Good.
That is the beauty of being an independent member like myself; I can be critical even of my own government.
It must be pretty bad when you criticize it.

I am going to mention the luxury taxes, because I feel there is discrimination against certain people. There are not many retailers in the House of Commons; therefore I am justified in bringing this to the attention of the minister. No doubt he had to decide this year-he does not take me into his confidence-what would be best for the country as a whole. In his judgment he decided that he should allow certain taxes to remain and to give, as he did, certain taxpayers reductions ranging from 29 per cent to 54 per cent. I should like to point out to him that the sales tax is spread over every commodity and over practically every type of sale. In addition he penalizes jewellers, furriers, the leather people and other trades. It is because of that discrimination that I draw his attention to the luxury tax, and I suggest to him that it should be looked into. Perhaps it is too late to do anything this year, but it should be looked into for the future in order to bring all on the same level.
I hold in my hand a brief which no doubt has been received by all hon. members. It comes from the Canadian Retail Federation. I have not had an opportunity of studying the particular sections referred to, but I do know the story well enough to refer to such items as the hon. member for Rosedale has already mentioned. A fountain pen is a very necessary thing in these days, and yet the Minister of Finance says that to use a fountain pen you must pay a 25 per cent additional tax. Clocks-some of us cannot get up in the morning without a clock-have a luxury tax
2S84
The Budget-Mr. Isnor

placed on them. Trunks, billfolds, shopping bags, are taxable; oil paintings, oriental rugs, and many' other items incidental to living in the way enjoyed by the hon. member for Rose-dale, are not taxed. That is why I say there is discrimination.
There is discrimination.
The minister is in the same high category.

My hearing is pretty good, but I cannot hear a whisper. I quote from the brief of the federation.
It has been suggested that the moment is inopportune to repeal the excise tax upon the items to which we have referred, because to do so would involve pressure from other groups who would demand similar treatment. If this argu-men is valid, it would appear to us that it would be applicable to any budget period-which gives rise to the fear that these so-called special wartime taxes are now to become part of our permanent economy.
I think the Minister of Finance will agree that these were purely wartime measures put on to prevent spending and an increase in the moneys that came into the hands of individuals. I quite agree that during war time that was justified.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: Revenue was needed too.
Cut out some of the extravagance.

1 do not think that revenue [DOT] was the really important point. Some of these items did not run into very many million dollars. I would point out to the Minister of National Revenue, and I do so in a kindly spirit, that there is a question whether it is wise from another angle. The great majority of our merchants in Canada keep proper records, but there are those, and there are such people in all classes, who evade this type of tax, and it is this type of tax that leads to evasion, rather than the regular sales tax, collected as it is in a fair manner. I hope the minister will bear that in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: We know that, and we have caught up with a lot of them.

I thought I would mention this as a duty to those who have presented the matter to me from time to time.
I was struck by an article I saw recently in the Financial Post. I generally look to the Financial Post to see what it has to say, since it leans to a great extent to the views of those whom some would call our Tory friends, but whom I prefer to describe as Conservatives. The Financial Post says that the Tories ask first to raise old age pensions, then eliminate the radio licence fees, then increase

agricultural floor prices-that, I believe, came from the leader of the opposition-then raise income tax exemptions, as the member for Rosedale suggested, and treat veterans more generously, just to mention a few of their suggestions; and in the same breath they ask that taxes be reduced.
Cut out the extravagance.
I would ask the hon. gentleman to look over the estimates and then point definitely to any extravagance so far as this government is concerned.
I have done it on more occasions than one.

I have referred to the statement of the Minister of Finance that the object of the budget was to encourage free enterprise. I do not know whether that is the best term these days. I prefer "progressive" enterprise. I looked up the word "enterprise" in the Oxford dictionary and I find this meaning given;
Enterprise: Undertaking, bold or difficult one, courage, readiness to engage.
The method of the enterprising is -to plan with audacity and execute with vigour; to sketch out a map of possibilities and then to treat them as probabilities.
That is what the Minister of Finance is doing in his budget-looking to the future, and giving the average taxpayer an opportunity to increase his spending power, thus keeping up employment and production, in which my Conservative friends are so greatly interested. I suggest that they should be supporting the budget to the limit instead of engaging in petty criticism.
May I say a word to those representing labour?-and I believe that in a measure I represent labour. I believe the real interest of labour lies with an independent economy rather than with socialism, which again and again has destroyed labour's opportunity. Organized labour has a greater stake in the private enterprise system than either management or capital; for that system is the union's chief hope of survival, and I say that without fear of contradiction by any of those who pose as leaders and supporters of the labour group.
I wish to throw out another constructive thought. I have nothing whatever to say about the social measures being brought out by this government. The country as a whole owes them a debt of gratitude for the manner in which they have enlarged social services, and with the additional social measures coming into operation I would hesitate to be the least bit critical, but I believe that we

The Budget-Mr. Isnor
can invest in undertakings that would be productive and self-liquidating. We could invest to a greater extent in that direction than we are now doing. I believe the country would do well to follow the advice that has been given, not from one source but from different quarters in this regard. The member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) brought up the question of irrigation as it applies to his particular section of the country, and other members from the west have also discussed the question. If it can be shown that such projects are self-liquidating, then I think the government would be well advised to undertake them. With that thought in mind I would ask the government to give serious consideration to greater investment in projects that might be undertaken in connection with breakwaters and wharves for the benefit of the fishermen along the Atlantic.
I could elaborate on that, but I think that one sentence covers the subject as well as it could be dealt with if I spent half an hour trying to make a stronger case.
I throw out these suggestions to the Minister of Finance, but I am not unmindful of the representations that have been made in the past and during recent years in regard to the marshlands of Nova Scotia. There is a wonderful opportunity to do some useful work that would add to the wealth of our province. If these projects are undertaken- fisheries and the marshlands-we can look forward to a greater degree of prosperity in the maritimes.
I am in accord with what has been said- and I do not hesitate to give him credit for having raised the question-by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) with reference to the Canso project. The question has also been raised from time to time by others. Last year the member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. McGarry) made a very strong appeal to the government in the matter. I am happy to associate myself with these gentlemen and other members who have brought this question to the attention of the government. I also associate myself with the member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Winters) who last night discussed subjects relating to Nova Scotia.
The member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) has been bringing up the question of the marshes for the last six years.

I said there were others.
The hon. member would not allow me to forget the member for Cumberland-
You would not forget him.

-and I am happy to fink his name with the others. I might even go
beyond that and look back to the period from 1940 to 1945 when the then member for Col-chester-Hants, Mr. Purdy, made such a strong plea. At that time the member for Cumberland joined Mr. Purdy in his representations.
What has been done about it?
It has been getting careful attention, and I am very hopeful.
Due consideration.
I am surprised at the hon. member for Royal laughing it off.
I was not laughing it off. I was laughing at your ancient history and nothing being done; that is all.
I for one am anxious to see these three projects undertaken, along with others.
