Thank you, sir. I was just going to make one more point in connection with the transfer of labour from the maritimes. It is unfortunate that such a thing has to take place. All members from Nova Scotia regret it. The hon. member for Colchester-Hants (Mr. Stanfield) will appreciate what has taken place so far as his own town is concerned. There is an article in to-day's Truro paper headed, "Shortage of materials affecting Truro's textile mills." It goes on to say that this company from Ontario, the Monarch Knitting Company, are now in the maritimes looking for women workers to be transferred to Ontario for employment. Truro is an aggressive and enterprising town. We are very fortunate to have here in the House of Commons a man of the type of the hon. member for Colchester-Hants. His firm has done a great deal for Nova Scotia and for Truro. I should hate to have the continued employment which he has given to the town of Truro affected by the transfer of workers or by people from Ontario being permitted to come in and take from him and from other manufacturers any of their skilled help. The manufacturers in Truro have done a wonderful job, not only for Truro but also for Nova Scotia and the whole of Canada. As an hon. member said to me one day about
The Budget-Mr. Blackmore

Stanfield's underwear, "It is right there on your breast, no doubt." The great majority of members are no doubt wearing it. Stanfield's underwear is sold from one end of Canada to the other. I suggest to the Minister of Labour and those on the government benches that they do not permit the transfer of labour from Nova Scotia but that instead they encourage to the greatest extent possible the purchase of products made in Nova Scotia and in the maritimes generally in order to increase employment in that part of the country.

Mr. Speaker, with at least two of the observations made by the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Isnor) I am in hearty accord. The first is that we should encourage all over Canada the establishment of self-liquidating projects and enterprises. The second is that the industry of this country should be decentralized. I wish to join with the hon. member in a protest against the way in which the industries of Nova Scotia and the maritimes have been undermined, weakened, destroyed and brought to the central provinces in times past. I wish to support him in the contention that these industries should be restored to the maritimes; and if it requires government assistance to accomplish that objective, I should be in favour of government assistance even though it does require expenditure.
This afternoon I had intended to speak about the matter of taxation and debt, but certain things which have occurred in the house have made me feel that it was my duty to leave those two topics for discussion at a later time and to turn my attention, and that of such members of the house as will follow me, to the problem of our beet sugar industry in this dominion.
At the present time we are in danger of losing 50,000,000 pounds of sugar production in 1947. I have brought that fact to the attention of the house two or three times already by means of questions. Let me once more draw the matter to the attention of the house and the country; it is not one which should be treated lightly. Last year, Canada and Dominion Sugar Company had 26,681 acres of beets signed up by contract. Of that number. 23,375 acres were harvested. They produced 70,000,000 pounds of beet sugar. Evidence for this can be found in Wellington Jeffers' article in the Globe and Mail of January 18, 1947.
Only yesterday, on May 7, hon. members heard the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Mayhew) announce that up to noon May 5, 
this sugar company has had signed up only 26,089 acres. It is quite obvious that the sugar company has not the chance this year to produce the amount of sugar that it had last, even if it has the exceptional weather conditions which favoured its efforts then.
The farmers are not signing up because they fear a shortage of labour. In 1946, 575 acres of beets were lost because there was not sufficient labour to care for them. Hon. members heard the announcement made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell): yesterday, but his announcement was like most of the announcements which have come from the government during the last few months with regard to the sugar industry-it was full of fallacies, misrepresentations and illusions.
For the information which I am going to give to the house this afternoon, I shall draw largely on a pamphlet entitled, "When can Ontario's Beet Sugar Production be Restored?" published by Canada and Dominion Sugar Company Limited, Chatham, Ont., in January, 1947. Hon. members will therefore know that the figures which I use are pretty . likely to be dependable.
It might not be generally known that Mr. S. R. Noble, sugar controller during the war, on January 27, 1947, told the joint delegation of the Canadian Sugar Beet Growers' Association and the Beet Sugar Processors of Canada that he was apprehensive of a more critical situation in Canada's sugar supply for the end of 1947 and the first half of 1948 than anything which has yet existed. Evidence for this will be found in a document entitled, "Notes on the dominion subsidy on domestic beet sugar production." I do not know how many hon. members have access to this document, but anyone interested may read the one in my possession. The document is signed by Mr. H. Sulkers, secretary of the Canadian Beet Producers' Association and other men prominent in the beet sugar business. Their signatures make the document authentic. In the light of the fact that Mr. Noble .told these gentlemen that solemn truth, I must say that I find myself completely at a loss to understand the indifferent attitude which the government is taking in the matter of signing up the remainder of these beet contracts for this year. There is plenty of labour in the country if the beet sugar industry can get it, and there is plenty of land available.
On May 7, as recorded at page 2845 of Hansard, the Minister of Labour made this remark:
I am not aware of any serious difficulties that occurred in 1946 because of competition between tobacco growers and those engaged in the rais-

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
ing of sugar beets. I am advised that the labour supply was adequate for both those branches of our agricultural economy.
It is quite evident that the minister had not gone into the problem far enough, or he would not have made a statement like that. May I tell hon. members some of the things that occurred last year, according to the information in my possession. Last year the Canada and Dominion Sugar Company sent out scouts to enlist labour for the beet fields. These scouts visited the counties of Norfolk and Simcoe and the Niagara peninsula, and had a considerable measure of success. At the Petrolia camp the company established a hostel to make it easier for those working in the beet fields to find accommodation, in order to encourage them to remain there. One day there were thirty beet workers, a cook and a helper at that hostel. The next day only the cook and helper were left; all the men had been lured away by the tobacco growers. How had they done this? They had offered the men higher wages than the beet raisers could afford, considering the relatively meagre income they were to receive from their beets. I am told the tobacco growers offered the men $125 a month, and in addition said they would give them work inside during the stormy weather. These attractions were simply beyond the power of the beet growers to meet, and as a result the men left. All a farmer has to do, if he is contemplating signing a beet contract or refusing to sign one, is to keep in mind one or two bitter experiences like that. All that is necessary is to see a part of that 575 acres of beets going to ruin because of lack of labour, to warn him off any possibility of signing a beet contract. There are, at best, so many risks involved in beet growing that he cannot afford to take an additional chance like that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I wonder if the hon. gentleman would put on record the last part of the statement I made in the house, starting with the words "Beet sugar production in Canada." Otherwise I think he will leave the impression that there has not been an increase in the production of beet sugar in Canada.

I thank the hon. gentleman. I was just going to do that, and by the time I get through I think he will prefer that I had not done so, because once more the statement is based on too little information. The minister meant well, but he did not have the whole picture. May I read from the statement of the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Mayhew) as recorded at page 2845 of Hansard for yesterday:
Beet sugar production in Canada in 1946 was 30 per cent greater than the average for 1935-39. This is a greater increase than that
of any other beet sugar producing country. Given at least average climatic conditions it is expected that production in Canada in 1947 will exceed that of 1946. In the light of these facts there can be no adverse reflection upon Canada's contribution to the world sugar position.
I now point out to the minister something which, in his busy life, he has probably not had an opportunity to investigate. What we are discussing at the present time is the production in Ontario, not the over-all production throughout Canada. It is quite true that in Alberta, where conditions in regard to the obtaining of labour were much more favourable, production was increased. There the competition of hoed crops, cash crops, with the beet sugar industry was not so intense as in Ontario, as I shall point out in the course of my remarks. In the Ontario scene, however, the picture is very disheartening indeed, as I think the minister will recognize in the light of the figures I shall put on Hansard in a moment. What we are discussing, let me repeat is the Ontario production, for it was in Ontario last year that 50,000,000 pounds of sugar which could have been produced were not produced, because not enough beets were available to supply both the Wallaceburg and Chatham factories, the consequence being that the Wallaceburg factory was left idle. The minister will also be interested to consider that there was a great deal of adverse comment in high places in the United States because of the fact that last year Canada produced so small a percentage of her sugar needs as compared with what she disposal. If Canada does no better this year could have produced with the capacity at her in comparison with what she could do, then I am afraid that adverse criticism in the United States will be much louder and more dangerous, and will be heard much higher up.
May I now give some figures to show the minister how serious has been the deterioration in the beet sugar industry in Ontario during the war years, since the administrator took over. Perhaps I ought to stop here and say that I do not wish to reflect too much on certain hon. gentlemen; but in considering the beet sugar situation since Mr. Noble took over as administrator I have had the impression that he has been deliberately designing the destruction of the beet sugar industry in Canada, and I cannot escape the conviction that he has been deliberately seeking to destroy the beet sugar industry in Ontario. I do not propose to bring before the house at the present time evidence to substantiate that allegation, but before this session is over I shall do so and give the administrator and all his friends opportunity to present a defence, if

Now, I think hon. members will be quite astonished when they hear of the devices which have been used to weaken, to choke out, to smother, to strangle the Ontario beet sugar industry. First, there were price ceilings. The price ceiling on sugar has been maintained so low in comparison with ceilings on other crops such as tomatoes, tobacco, beans and corn, that the beet sugar industry has been placed at a serious disadvantage. The price ceiling on beet sugar was brought in at a relatively early period, and has been rather consistently maintained. I am not objecting to the establishment of price ceilings. It was well that the Canadian people should have been able to buy their sugar at a low rate, but the difference should have been made up by the government to the sugar factories or the sugar companies by way of a subsidy, which would have enabled them to carry on and expand without causing the people to suffer. This is an extremely important matter. Another device used was subsidies given to competing crops such as corn, peas, beans, tomatoes and perhaps tobacco, although I doubt there was a subsidy on tobacco. Subsidies were given to these other crops which put them in an advantageous position in competition with the beet sugar industry as regards available labour. This has had a serious effect, being one of the factors which brought about the closing of the Wallaceburg plant during several of the war years.

Another thing has been done about which the ordinary man on the street or even the ordinary member of parliament knows nothing. The beet sugar companies customarily have sold their sugar on the basis of delivered-to-the-trade. They usually have sold their beet sugar in the winter time when rates of transportation on the lakes were higher than in the summer. But the price was fixed on the basis of the lower summer rates. That bled a little more out of the beet sugar industry of Ontario. Not very much blood needs to drip away from a person's body in any given minute to constitute a fearful drain provided that it continues long enough. This drain has been going on constantly during the war years and I am told it is still going on. Hon. members will find this discussed on page 5 of the pamphlet to which I referred.
Prices are the really vital factors which affect the stability of any factory and certainly prices have seriously affected the stability of the beet sugar factories. I should like to quote some figures to show hon. members what has been happening with respect to prices and how it has affected the sugar beet industry in Ontario. But price was a factor, the only really vital factor, as is shown by comparison with tomatoes and tobacco, both of which increased in acreage as prices increased, despite the fact that the labour requirements of these crops are fully equal to sugar beets.
In that statement a sad story is conveyed. Supporters of the government in the house, and in radio programmes over the air, have been endeavouring to impress upon the people that the reason the beet sugar industry was not doing so well was that it was not 83166-184
able to compete successfully. How can an industry compete when its hands are tied; and not only when its hands are tied, but when its feet are tied-"hog-tied", as we say in the west.
I turn now to the labour costs aspect of the question. With net returns on sugar beets up thirty-six per cent, labour costs have grown as follows: in 1941, $18 per acre, and in 1945, $33 per acre, or almost double. That is an increase of $15, or eighty-three per cent. The rise in labour cost per acre is greater by over thirty per cent than the rise in net return to the farmer, even including the Ontario provincial subsidy.
I turn to the question of losses through various other kinds of manipulation, which have been exercised to the detriment of the beet sugar industry. I refer to page 9. Two by-products of the beet sugar industry which are of considerable importance are beet pulp and beet molasses. The Canada and Dominion Sugar Company sells dried beet pulp I am told; most of the other companies sell the beet pulp wet. Dry beet pulp, and molasses from beets, constitute two lucrative by-products which greatly add to the general profitability of the beet sugar industry.
Let us see what managers in Canada have done in respect of these two important items. About two-thirds of the dried beet pulp from Ontario in pre-war years was sold in the United States. As from 1941, the Ontario company was directed by the Ottawa feeds controller to sell the product for feed in Canada. In January, 1947, the difference between prices in the United States and those in Canada was as follows: The Canadian ceiling price f.o.b. plant is $26.40 a ton, while the United States price, f.o.b. Michigan plant, just across the border, is $49.40 a ton, or almost twice as much; and the differential against the Canadian producer is $23 a ton.
A similar situation prevails with respect to beet molasses. The Canadian ceiling price f.o.b. plants is $28.75 a ton, and the United States price f.o.b. Michigan plants is $38 a ton, or a differential against the Canadian producer of $9.25.
All that is to be remembered is that the amount of money which the company was able to derive from some of these by-products entered into the amount it paid the farmers for the production of their beets. So that when the company was restricted in its income from the sale of these two by-products it was necessarily restricted in the amount of money it could pay the farmer for producing beets; consequently the farmer was automatically restricted in the amount he could pay for labour.

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore

In 1941 the total Ontario production of beet molasses was 15,628 tons, of which 10,475 tons, or sixty-seven per cent, was shipped to the United States. A similar percentage of beet pulp was shipped to that country. However, of the 1946 output a relatively small percentage was allowed to be exported to the United States.
Under ceiling prices, pulp is relatively cheaper than other cattle feeds, so that the demand has grown in Canada under price control. The demand for beet molasses has also grown in Canada. It is used in the manufacture of yeast, citric acid, and many other products.
Hon. gentlemen will ask if I would advocate that the price should have been allowed to rise, or if I would have favoured keeping prices down for 'Canadian stock feeders. Well, obviously I would agree that the cattle producer or stock producer in Canada should have 'been able to get feed cheaply. But that is no reason why the producer of beet pulp should have been penalized. There should have been, I say again, a substantial subsidy which would have made up to the Canadian producer that which he lost because his product was under a ceiling price; but no such subsidy was forthcoming. The dictator who presided as administrator over Canadian sugar concerns just would not listen as regards any of these matters. The result has been that an important Canadian industry has suffered.
I believe that is sufficient on that aspect of the matter. Meanwhile, while all these other adverse developments have been in progress, processing costs have been rising rapidly. Notwithstanding all the considerations I have mentioned, we have people like the Minister of Justice (Mr. Usley), who will rise in their places and try to convey to the house and the country that this industry would require altogether too much by way of subsidies and too much tariff protection in order
to survive. How can one describe such an attitude? One cannot possibly characterize it properly without violating the rules in respect of parliamentary good taste.
(Mr. Blackmore.]
There is another aspect which, while not so important, has had its serious effect, since the closing of the Wallaceburg plant. Obviously farmers who produce beets are located throughout the areas in which the Wallaceburg and Chatham plants are situated. When one of those plants is closed, then farmers must transport their produce some considerable distance in order to deliver it to the other plant. The sugar factory had to absorb this cost. I am told that the farmer was paid on the delivered-to-the-factory basis. This is found in the pamphlet to which I referred. Thus the company has had. to absorb this loss. Then, too, the company has had to finance subsidies from delivery of beets to the factory to the time of payment for the sugar. In order that hon. members may understand this situation, let me point out that certain subsidies were being paid on the beets, and the factory generally paid those subsidies about the time the beets were delivered. Then, until the sugar was sold the factory could not get reimbursement from the government for the amount it had paid out. The result was that the factory became a sort of banker for the government during six or eight months of the year. Just think of that, for an outrage!
Yet, would the sugar administrator listen? Would the Minister of Finance listen? Would the chairman of the wartime prices and trade board listen? No, not they. They would not listen to this or to any other of these problems, or provide any sort of remedial measure. No wonder the province of Ontario had to step in, with its own provincial subsidies, to save the sugar industry in that province from complete destruction.
The beet sugar industry throughout the war came to the dominion government time after time with well-reasoned briefs-moderate, scientific and factual-and asked certain considerations. Never once have the beet sugar people been given what they have asked for. This year of 1947 was no exception. On January 27, and dates following, the combined beet producers and beet processors of Canada met government officials-first the sugar administrator, and then others-and presented their case. Mr. Sulkers, secretary of the Canadian Beet Growers' Association, asked that an additional subsidy of SI.08 be allowed beyond the 60J cents given in 1946, because, said Mr. Sulkers, "the administrator is going to pay eight-five cents a ton more for his raw canes from abroad than he was paying in 1946. If he is to give us parity he must increase the price which we are to receive, and this is what we compute to be the increase which he ought to give us". Would!

The Budget-Mr. Blackmore
the sugar administrator listen to that? Not he. Would the Minister of Finance listen? (Not he.
The beet people asked for certain subsidiary advantages not difficult to give. They asked that the controls be lifted on dried beet pulp and on molasses or the raising of the ceiling price. (Here I would point out, there could have been a subsidy to make up for what they wished.) It was refused. Molasses was decontrolled shortly after, but I do not know that it was because these people asked for it; it may have been.
In addition, they asked that an allotment of three pounds of sugar per ton of beets delivered be given to the man who delivered the beets, up to 200 pounds or up to 100 pounds. The idea behind this suggestion was that a man farming would be encouraged to produce three or four acres of beets to a farm in order to be able to get the additional sugar. It is an obvious device. It would not have cost the government anything. The man, before he got his additional three pounds per ton of sugar, would have produced a ton of beets, and about 300 lbs. of sugar. Would these wiseacres we had in authority in Canada agree with that request? Not at all; that would have been to intelligent for them. They would rather leave the sugar unproduced, which they are doing.
The beet men asked that the factories be not required to finance the subsidies between the delivery of the beets and the sale of the sugar, but that was denied. May I read to the house a statement from the document to which I referred a short time ago, prepared by the beet people and signed by Mr. Sulkers. I read from the bottom of page 2 as follows:
It was represented with all the vigour at the command of the various spokesmen that maximum domestic beet sugar production would not be achieved in 1947 unless the sugar administrator set his sights considerably higher by way of subsidy.
There is no excuse for the sugar administrator; there is no excuse for the Minister of Finance; there is no excuse for the government. The whole situation was made abundantly clear to them.
Let me now point out two or three other aspects of this question which are serious. In the main, Canada's sugar supply comes from the international sugar pool. Yesterday the hon. member for Victoria, B.C., pointed out that we got our sugar supply from the international pool. That is granted, but practically the dominating factor in the sugar pool is the United States of America. According to information which I have, the United States government bought the whole of the 83166-184J
Cuban 1947 crop, which is the important element, the deciding factor in the whole situation. They bought the whole of the crop for 1947. The United States therefore controls it. Let the United States once get the idea that Canada simply does not intend to play her part, that she does not mean to play ball, what would be the obvious decision and conclusion of the United States? I say that, as matters stand, our whole sugar situation in the year 1947-48 is in jeopardy.
There is another aspect of this question which should have a little attention before I close. Much has been said against beet sugar because it requires tariff protection. The argument is advanced all over the country that the industry should not be allowed to survive because it needs tariff protection. Let us look at the tariff protection which some other agricultural products have. Take barley. One would hardly think barley required protection in Canada. Barley has a twenty-five cents a bushel protection under the general tariff and 22i under the intermediate tariff. Beef has four cents a pound protection under the British preferential tariff, eight cents a pound under the general tariff and six cents a pound under the intermediate tariff. Butter has eight cents a pound protection under the British preference and fourteen cents a pound under the general tariff, twelve cents under the intermediate tariff. I could go on and give a list that comprises practically every commodity which Canada produces on her farms. Look at the protection we have to give to our butter. No one can manufacture and sell oleomargarine in Canada because it comes into competition with butter!

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext: Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but his time has expired.

I do not wish to encroach on the time of the house. I will simply close by urging that without further delay the government go to work on this problem and devise means whereby the men who would sign up to raise sugar beets for the Dominion Sugar Company shall be guaranteed their labour, and whatever other encouragement they require.

The budget is a subject of great concern to the people of Canada, most of whom were disappointed in it, because some of the taxes that were on might have been taken off, and because some so-called nuisance taxes, as they are known, were not abolished. I am thinking particularly of the heavy taxes on soft
The Budget-Mr. Drove

drinks and chocolate bars which are largely purchased by the youth of our land. It would seem, now that the war is over, that these taxes might be discontinued. The radio licence should also be abolished. The tax of twenty-five per cent on silverware which was put on during the war, was imposed, if the former Minister of Finance (Mr. Ilsley) is reported correctly, with the idea of discouraging production. This tax has served its purpose, which was to discourage the use of critical materials needed for war purposes. Surely there is no need to continue this argument now that the war has been over for two years. Many veterans and young couples are attempting to establish their homes. Knives and forks are a necessity which should not be subject to a luxury tax of twenty-five per cent.
The special excise tax discriminates between one type of retail sale and another and, in effect, is discriminatory. For example, a refrigerator is taxable; an icebox is not. An electric range is taxable; a coal range is not. Clocks, watches, shopping bags, et cetera, are taxable, while oil paintings, oriental rugs and many other items incidental to luxury living are not taxable. It has been suggested that the moment is inopportun- to repeal the extra tax on the items to which I have referred, because to do so would involve protests from other groups who would demand similar treatment. If this argument is valid it would appear to me that it would be applicable to any budget period, which gives rise to the fear that these so-called special wartime taxes are now to become part of our permanent economy. In my opinion it is most desirable, in the interest of maintaining reasonable business confidence, that these irritating and discriminatory taxes should be removed.
The Post Office Department appears to be making considerable money. Apparently it had a surplus of over $10 million last year. Is it not time that consideration be given to bringing the postal rate back to three cents instead of the four-cent rate which has been in effect for some time. I do not think it was the intention that the post office should be a money-making concern; rather it should be a service to the people at cost.
The price of dairy products is of great concern to the people of Northumberland county as well as to the majority of Canadians. Prices have been supported1 by subsidies and ceiling prices have been put on many products. The last announcement of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) on behalf of the government is, in my opinion, most unsatisfactory. On May 1, the ceiling price on butter

was raised ten cents. If it was the intention of the government to assure reasonable prices to the producers a floor price should have been established at the same time. We have reached the time of year in this country when production exceeds consumption in butter; therefore it is necessary for someone to carry surplus butter during the summer months, which is the high production season. It is unreasonable to expect that any buyer will pay the ceiling price and carry butter for several months only to sell it at the same ceiling price. Producers of butter fat have been placed in an impossible position by this government paying higher amounts for other dairy products, and thereby cream producers are placed at a disadvantage as compared with others.
This situation was accepted during the war, but it is surely unreasonable to expect that it should now be continued. It is owing to wrong government policy that it is necessary to import several million pounds of New Zealand butter, which should have been sent to the British people, who are so greatly in need of fats. Moreover, I understand that some 38,808 pounds of this butter have not been sold in this country after having been brought in.
All the butter that is required could be produced in this country if the producers received a reasonable price. As a result of the present government's policy, consumers are paying more for butter and, producers are receiving less. If the ceiling price and rationing are to be continued, a better floor price should be put on products to assume farmers reasonable prices. The cheese producers are not satisfied with the price they are receiving. The minister announced the other day that he would take all cheese at the floor price. Surely this is discouraging to the cheese producers, to hear that the government are going to take all their cheese at the floor price.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: We did not announce that.

If it is necessary to sell at less, then the farmers should be paid a better price and the difference carried by all the people of Canada. A prosperous agriculture will provide one of the best markets for our manufactured goods, and everything possible should be done to assure a reasonable return for our basic industries.

I am going to contribute my little bit to this debate. This is not a large or enthusiastic house. The budget, which has been played up both by the Minister of

The Budget-Mr. Gillis
Finance (Mr. Abbott) and by the members who have spoken from that side of the house, is, in my opinion, a complicated document. To make an analysis of that budget from the financial point of view, under the mechanics of things as they are today, is not a realistic approach to it.
At this time I am not going to make a financial analysis of the budget. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), speaking in this debate, spoke for this group, and I think he went pretty thoroughly into the financial ramifications of the budget. I am in hearty accord with what he said, and I believe that even from that point of view he pretty well exploded the airy pronouncements of the Minister of Finance.
I am going to attempt to tell the house what I think of this budget as viewed by the man in the street, and you cannot discuss this budget realistically without relating it to the rapid increases in the cost of living, because in the final analysis what the dollar will buy for the average man is the thing that counts. Giving him slight tax relief here and there and then taking 100 per cent back from him by increasing his cost of living and lowering his standards is not relief, and that is why I say it is tricky. Viewed as it was reviewed by the headlines of the press, the budget is likely to appear to people as having done something. In my opinion the reverse is true.
Let me mention this in passing, for example. Working the relief out on a percentage basis, taking the statement in the press that the lower income groups were relieved by fifty-four per cent, let us see what that actually means to the man who receives $150 a month and who has a couple of children-and that is about the average across the country, if we take those who are employed and are paying taxes. That fifty-four per cent means a relief of nineteen cents a week. That man eats every week; he pays bills every week, and he saves nineteen cents by that fifty-four per cent reduction. Then the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) comes along the next day and announces an increase of ten cents a pound on butter. The average family, or the family I have been discussing in that $150 income group, will consume about 2-3 pounds of butter a week. Therefore the Minister of Finance the night before gave him a relief of nineteen cents and the Minister of Agriculture took twenty-three cents from him the following day.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: The last member said they didn't pay it.

The group I am talking about does. So that this man is four cents worse off so far as the actual purchasing power of the dollar, or the standard of living, is concerned than he was before the budget was announced. That is on that one item of food alone. Of course, fifty per cent of our wage-earners are in the group that pays no taxes at all. These people have not sufficient income to pay taxes. Well, the fellow who does not pay taxes is twenty-three cents a week worse off than before the minister brought down his budget, because the Minister of Agriculture, in that one item of food alone, threw back upon him twenty-three cents and he got no relief. He is that much worse off.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Suppose the Minister of Agriculture had made his announcement first.

It would not make any difference, but it was timed very well for political purposes. The Minister of Finance gets headlines to the effect that he is relieving those in the low-income groups, while the Minister of Agriculture might not have been noticed in the ballyhoo there was in the press about the budget. His announcement may not have been noticed; perhaps it has not been noticed to any great extent except by members who are trying to police the standard of living of the Canadian people.
I think what would have been more realistic on the part of the government would have been to step up the exemptions to the figures mentioned by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. That would have done away with the necessity for returns. For this group that has suffered a decrease in its standard of living under this budget, plus increases in prices, it would have obviated the necessity of filing any income tax returns, and that in turn would have saved the government a large amount of money in administration expenses. If the government had wanted to do something for the lower income group, and that is the group for which something has to be done, that is the sort of action which should have been taken. This filing of income tax returns, every member will agree, is one of the greatest yearly headaches, and the chap who is not getting anything at all by way of relief and who has to continue filing that return finds himself worse off at the end of the year than before the budget was brought down. If the suggestion I make had been followed, this chap would at least have been saved this headache of filing returns and the government would have got rid of much surplus staff which they have checking returns that do not mean very much to anyone.
The Budget-Mr. Gillis

Of course the worst beating that people in the low-income groups have taken during the last year has been that increase in the cost of living. I have here a clipping from the Ottawa Journal of May 4, which does not bear out many statements one hears with regard to increases in prices. This clipping states-and these are official figures too:
The cost of living index, reeling under the impact of higher prices, advanced 1-7 points during March to 130-6 at April 1-the biggest jog in the line since 1941-the Dominion Bureau of Statistics reported on Saturday.
This is dated May 4. Continuing:
Higher food prices accounted for most of the increase, while clothing and home furnishings also contributed to the unprecedented rise.
The bureau's food index mounted from 148-7 on March 1, to 151-6 as beef, sugar, vegetables and fruits were chalked up higher in grocery stores across the dominion. Price increases for a broad range of clothing items advanced the index from 133-1 to 136-9.
Anyone who tries to argue that the low-income groups in this country have received any relief from this budget is either badly informed or trying to fool somebody; because, in the final analysis, by this action alone- by the removal of price controls and by the removal of subsidies-the low-income groups have taken a terrific licking, and the budget offers to them no relief in any way, shape or form. That is the way it affects the man in the street, as he will find when he has had time to analyse it. That budget, if it was brought down for political purposes, will certainly not draw any water to the mill of the government.
I want to devote most of the time at my disposal in this debate to .the part of the country from which I come. I hear members of the house say, "The C.C.F. is talking depression; they would welcome a depression; they are going to bring on a depression." May I say that some of the most outstanding economists in North America today are writing books on the subject and, if they know anything about it, they forecast a trend in that direction within the next few years. But at this time I am not going to talk about the general trend. I wish to inform the Minister of Finance and the members of this house, particularly the maritime members, that the maritime provinces have already struck a depression. They have been in the throes of a depression for the last year, and from an economic point of view they are today in as bad a condition as they were in at any time during the depression which preceded this war. I wish to compliment the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Winters), who spoke last evening. Not enough of the maritime members, particularly those on the

government side of the house, approach the matter as courageously as he did. By figures which I am not going to bother quoting again, he definitely pointed out the inequality in the distribution of the wealth of this country, as it applies to the maritime provinces. They are, as it were, the step-children of confederation. He did a realistic job.
There are one or two things, however, on which I do not agree with him. He said that one of the main considerations in dominion-provincial relations was the right of the province to retain certain small taxing fields. I do not agree with that statement. I think the tax agreements were a minor item when placed alongside other problems involved in dominion-provincial relations, such as, for example, the question of social security as contained in the original proposals made by the dominion government to the provinces. We cannot forget that most of the people in this country are suffering from the want of medical attention because they cannot afford to pay for it. That applies right across the dominion, with the exception of Saskatchewan, in which province a health programme has been instituted with regard to which some progress has been made. But, generally speaking, you can have as much health in this country as you can buy, under present circumstances; and no more or no less. In their original submissions, the dominion government did propose to institute a health programm-e. The thing we do not want to forget is that we have a large number of people between the ages of sixty-five and seventy who would, have obtained some relief under the original proposals. They are calling for it. I think every member of this house, if he visits his constituency occasionally, will have the same experience that I had. I have had women come in, particularly those who had raised families and had given them to the nation, had lost them overseas-some came back but cannot secure employment-with no income whatsoever and no home, wondering when the old age pension is to be brought down to sixty-five years and take them in. That is a question which would have been settled under dominion-provincial relations. Lack of security is one of the things which is responsible for most of the isms that creep into a country.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: And I will talk to you, too.	[DOT]

I shall have a lot to say; and after we get through the minister may not be as cocky as he is now.
I was talking about the mothers who had contributed sons to the services which saved the institutions of this country in order that we may sit in seats of this kind and grow fat. These are the people I am talking about. I am talking about dominion-provincial relations, and I am not giving our own premier in Nova Scotia much credit for the quibbling that has been done on this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He is a very fine man.
Yes; he is a good Tory.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He is a very fine progressive Liberal.

He is a good Tory. Just a few days ago I noticed an item in the Globe and Mail, which said that Premier Duplessis stood up in his place in Quebec and deprecated the fact that Premier Macdonald was being insulted. He considered that himself, Drew and Macdonald were the future saviours of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You had better leave Macdonald alone.
Nobody can use abusive language better than Mr. Duplessis.

A person is known by the company he keeps. You have that group which I have mentioned which has received no relief from this budget, and who are panhandling a living, as it were, after contributing their all to the nation. That problem might have been solved under dominion-provincial relations.
I said a moment ago that fear is the thing which breeds most of the isms in a country. The Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) a short time ago deprecated the fact that there are several groups in this house. What
brought them her*? It was the failure of the old-line parties to solve the problems of this country. They are the original protesters against the inactivity of those entrusted with the management of the affairs of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: They are in great minority.

They will flourish and grow to the extent that you people continue the policy which you have had for the last seventy-five years and which, as far as I can see, you have not changed in any respect, not even in this budget. As to the average man who today produces the wealth of this coun-try_and this goes for the farmer, the fisherman and for every industrial worker-fear is the thing which drives him away from the machines that have exploited him in the past. It is fear of old age, after he has slaved and worn himself out on a farm or in industry, with nothing ahead of him but the scrap heap by way of social security in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Governments cannot cure
old age.

But you can provide for
it, just as you provide for judges and everyone else in the government service. It is the government's function to provide for it. You are squawking because communism is developing in the country, but you fail to provide for those who built this country and produced its wealth.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
May I point out to
hon. members that twenty-five years ago we had sixty-five members down in that corner, and what have w'e now?

Well, what is here today
is solid, and we are going to stay here and fight this battle to its conclusion. I say, to the extent you 'continue to legislate for fear in the hearts and minds of the people who produce the wealth of this country, to that extent groups such as this will grow and eventually take power in Canada. All you have to do is look across the ocean to Great Britain, Australia and New Zealand, where the modern mechanics of government are being applied to their resources for the alleviation of human misery rather than the amassing of wealth. I said the average farmer and worker feared old age, which means they have to go to the scrap heap. We see thousands of them in this country hobbling around on sticks, with no chance for medical attention. They cannot get in a hospital because they cannot pay for it. Many of them are worn out prematurely. They cannot qualify for that pauper's allowance called the old age
The Budget-Mr. Gillis

pension, so they just wait the streets or depend on what some member of the family may be able to give them.

speechtext: There was never a citizen of Canada denied hospitalization because he could not pay for it.

speechtext: It is the best country in the world.

I do not know anything
about what the minister has just said, but I know that I have had to take veterans of the first war to a hospital in a car, and become personally responsible for the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue; Minister of National War Services
speechtext: Where?

In the part of the country
from which I come, and it is no different from the rest of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Does my hon. friend
suggest for one second that the veterans of Canada are not better looked after than the veterans of any other country in the world today?
I am saying that maintenance allowances and everything else applying to the veterans should be increased fifty per cent and they would not be too well taken care of.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
We all agree with
that, but last year this country spent $807,000,000 for the care and after-care of veterans in Canada. That was spent by 12,000,000 people, and I think it was pretty decent, generous action on the part of the people.

Well, as I told you in your
veterans affairs committee and your pension committee, the solution is not to dump all the social security problems upon the veterans affairs department. Other legislation is necessary in this country to augment it. You are handling many problems-

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Who started it?

You are handling many problems in connection with veterans of the first war because there is no place else to send them. You generously do what you can for them, but other social security measures should be applied in this country to care for them, because in the final analysis they are not war service disabilities but disabilities of the ordinary citizens of this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is part of the programme of the government.

Yes, but it is class legislation. You can do something about it for the veterans, while many thousands of citizens of this country are denied any relief for the same 
disabilities. I was talking about fear because of lack of security. You live in fear from the day you start to work until you go to the grave; and what does the average worker in this country do for most of his lifetime? He tries to carry a SI,000 life insurance policy so that his family may be sure there will be enough money to bury him after he dies He is afraid to die; he is afraid of leaving a family to the tender mercies of an unknown future without his protecting hand. The minister wants to travel a bit in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I have travelled it far more than my hon. friend has. I can tell him that I have been in ten times more places in Canada than he has.
Well, I did not travel in a private car, at the expense of the taxpayers.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Nor did I. I travelled through the Peace river country by canoe in 1923.
You should take a spy-glass with you.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I travelled this country as an immigrant. My hon. friend can never hurl that accusation at me.
Well, I am hurling it. You travelled on the wrong side of the tracks.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I know more about the picture than you do.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I would ask hon. members not to interrupt the hon. gentleman who is speaking.
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. The minister is a bit touchy this afternoon. Either he is getting a little old, or his conscience is bothering him.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: You would like to get into a private car yourself.
I did travel in a private car, but the caption on the door of the car was "Twelve horses or forty men."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I travelled in that car, too.
It was a private car, and I was never ashamed of it.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: But you would like to get into one of the other kind, too.

I am not so sure. I'll tag along with the rank and file. I was trying to describe a condition to men who have never had any fear of insecurity, and who have never experienced any of the fears I have been trying to point out. I was going on to say that if the Prime Minister is afraid of

The Budget

Mr. Gillis
groups developing in this country, a situation which he does not like, the thing for him to do is remove that fear from the minds and hearts of the working people by a proper overall social security plan. That will remove it; and you need not be afraid of taxing people for such a plan, either. I had the privilege, for twenty-six years, of working as hard as anyone in this house has worked. I was never afraid of paying taxes. When I had an income that put me in the income tax bracket I was quite satisfied; and I was never afraid of being taxed for the purpose of providing security. I have taken part in meetings for twenty odd years. I have helped write pension acts and insurance acts which we tried to sell to the government of our province or to the corporation for which we worked. We were quite willing to pay our proportionate share of those security measures, but we could never get anyone to go along with us on them. If you are providing something in return for that tax the working people of this country will not be afraid to pay it, but they have not the opportunity.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
