The house resumed at eight o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I was doing my best to make everybody on the other side of the house as mad as possible. For the remainder of my time I am going to be specific and try not to tramp on anyone's corns. At six o'clock I was pointing out that the budget could not be properly analysed as to the benefits accruing to the people of Canada unless it was checked with the increasing cost of living. It is no use giving a person something with one hand and taking it away from him with the other. The hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Winters) stated on Tuesday evening that he came from a riding largely made up of people engaged in the fishing industry, and he said that the fishermen of his constituency would approve the present budget. That might be so if one relies on the press, particularly the headlines in certain sections of the country, but I still submit that the fishermen, on both the east and west coasts, is still the forgotten man. I have a few figures which will illustrate the position of the fishermen, on the east coast at least. The prices for fish quoted in Halifax on May 3 were as follows:
Cents per pound
Cod	 21
Haddock	 41
Halibut	 16 to 20
That is what the fisherman received. On the same day chain stores in Ottawa were offering fish at the following prices:
Cents per pound
Cod, frozen	 37
Smoked fillet	 39
Halibut	 42
There is a terrific spread between what the man who goes to sea to catch the fish and undergoes most of the hardship is receiving under present price ceilings and what the consumer in central Canada is paying. I am not going to go into the fisheries question in detail, but I should like to refer to a brief put out by the fisheries council of Canada, located at Ottawa. They make a few recommendations which I think should be checked and implemented as soon as possible. One is:
The "Act for the Support of the Prices of Fisheries Products" approved by parliament on August 15, 1944, has not as yet been made effective.
The fisheries council desires to urge upon the government the importance of proclaiming this legislation at the earliest possible date. The council's views of this important subject are amplified later in this brief and now may be summarized as follows:
1.	Early proclamation of the act.
2.	Board to contain representatives of the industry.
3.	Use of funds available to promote long term benefits to the fishermen rather than as relief payments or the dole.
I suggest that the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Bridges) should proclaim that act at the first opportunity so that it may become operative.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: How much of the difference between what is paid to the producer and what the consumer in Ottawa pays is absorbed by transportation costs?
I have not figured it out, but I imagine there is quite a lot of it.
And the processing.

However I think it is something the Minister of Fisheries should take up. The act should be proclaimed and the necessary machinery set up. At the present time, with the prices the fishermen are receiving, they are not able to maintain a standard of living equal to that of those in the rest of Canada who are steadily employed. Some effort should be made to set up the necessary machinery whereby the fisherman will get a

The Budget-Mr. Gillis

reasonable share of the national income. He is certainly working as hard as anyone else in this country.
I should like to say something more with regard to prices, to the Minister of Finance. There is an agitation right across the country for the removal of the tax on soft drinks in order to bring the bottle of pop back to a nickel, and there is also the chocolate bar problem. These two nuisance taxes should be removed, but if they are removed an effort should be made to see that prices do not go up rather than come down.
I wonder if the hon. member has examined the balance sheets of the soft drink and chocolate manufacturers? I have examined them and I am surprised the hon. member is advocating what he is.

I am not advocating the removal of these taxes for the benefit of manufacturers of soft drinks and chocolate bars; I am advocating their removal for the benefit of the children who purchase them. I have no more faith than has the hon. member that the larger manufacturers will not shove prices up rather than bring them down, but in the soft drink industry there are a number of small manufacturers in whom I have confidence, and I believe they would pass on that saving to the consuming public. Some control would have to be exercised by the government over the larger ones in order to see that prices were brought down.
I want to say a few words about the depressed condition of the maritimes, and I am going to be as unprovocative as possible. Most people in central Canada, particularly in Quebec and Ontario, when they hear us talking about employment in the maritimes and asking for subventions, are apt to say, "You want this, that or the other thing," and believe that they are giving us something. The reverse is true. When the maritime provinces entered confederation they were the most prosperous part of Panada, and the statesmen' of that time hesitated about coming into confederation. The fears which they expressed at that time were well founded because, after confederation, everything that existed in that part of the country that was wealth producing began to be siphoned into central and western Canada.
I want to show the house what was taken from the maritimes, and I am going to speak only about Nova Scotia. I shall let the New Brunswick members speak for themselves. I do not intend to go back beyond forty or fifty years. I say this because I have always looked upon governments, both federal
'.Mr. Gillis.]
and provincial, as trustees of the resources of the country, who would supervise their exploitation so that the greatest value to every section of the country might result from that exploitation.
The picture I see today in Nova Scotia is largely attributable to Liberal government; because it will be remembered that we have not had Conservative governments on many occasions since confederation in that province.
Bad luck for Nova Scotia.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Very lucky.

The fact of the matter is that we have not any representatives in the present legislature of Nova Scotia from that party. At least the Liberals have sense enough in that province not to get wrapped up in the other party, and become contaminated, as they have in western Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: You get good government in Nova Scotia.

Here is how good it has been, as I see it. As I said a moment ago, I am not going back very far. A Liberal government had been custodian of our resources during the period I am going to mention. And what did we lose to central Canada? I should like the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor)-the only member from that city at the present time-to pay attention to what I am saying, because he waxed most eloquent this afternoon on how good things were in that part of the country.
Fifty years ago we lost control of our finances. At that time we had the Merchants Bank, the Bank of Nova Scotia, the Halifax Banking Company, the Commercial Bank of Windsor, and the Union Bank of Halifax. Maritime capital was being applied to the resources of that province for the purpose of developing it. But all the control of her finances is now in Montreal and Toronto.
What happened to those five banks?

They were amalgamated, or siphoned off. Try to get money from them today to develop an industry in Nova Scotia which competes with something up here, and find out what happens. They hamstring you. He who controls finance, controls the country.
In addition to that, we lost industry. We lost a cotton mill at Halifax, and one at Windsor. We lost a paint works at Halifax, and three tobacco factories. We lost four or five shoe factories which were employing people, and the people they employed were spending money in Nova Scotia. We lost two silk factories and several woollen mills. We lost a cheese factory at Antigonish, and a

The Budget-Mr. Gillis
fairly large one at that. We lost a cement works which drifted into a merger, and came into Quebec. We lost a large fertilizer plant at Sydney, and a tinplate plant operated by Shaw and Mason of Sydney. We lost a large tar and chemical plant from Sydney. We lost a skate factory at Dartmouth, and a sugar refinery from the same place during the war. We lost a nut and bolt plant which employed 1,500 men, and had been a peacetime industry for some thirty years. It left there in 1943. We lost shipyards at Pictou and a plate mil! at Sydney. The Minister of Reconstruction and Supply (Mr. Howe) will remember that one. It employed 600 men during the war and it is not operating now. I hope to sell it in the near future, though.
That is the picture showing how well they managed it. That is the way the east has been depressed. That is why there are 30,000 unemployed.
Are there 30,000 unemployed in Nova Scotia?

In the maritimes; 15,000 of them are in Nova Scotia. If any business employed that kind of manager for two years, and he showed that kind of record in his balance sheet, on the assets side of his ledger, what would happen? They would put him into gaol for about thirty years; and rightly so.
They would make him a Liberal member of parliament.

We hear a lot about planning. What does it mean to that part of the country? We have lost all that wealth. We do not quarrel so much about what somebody else may have as we do about the control they may exercise over our natural resources, thereby stopping the creation of new wealth. This is the kind of thing that is doing it- centralization in the two central provinces in connection with the financing of industry, and because the distributing organizations are able to keep the east and west depressed, at their will. It is the control they exercise which we complain about mostly.
But they say that private enterprise is planning. Here is the planning they are doing; and it means precious little relief they will bring to the maritime provinces. These statistics are taken from page 9 of the forecast for 1947 on investment by Canadian business, which was made by the Department of Reconstruction and Supply, and tabled in the house a month or so ago by the minister of that department.
In 1947 they plan to spend $1,066,458,000. That is a lot of money. Where are they going to spend it? They are going to spend 83166-185J	j
five per cent of it in the maritimes; they are going to spend 26-7 per cent in Quebec; they are going to spend fifty per cent in Ontario; they are going to spend eight per cent in the prairie provinces, and they are going to spend ten per cent in British Columbia.
Your free enterprisers, who have money to invest, will spend the most of it in the two central provinces, with the complete centralization which they have today. The east and the west will remain the overseers of the poor, as they have been for a good many years.

speakerposition: Speaker of the Senate
speechtext:
Order. I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but I must remind him that he has exhausted his time.
Some hon. MEMBERS.: Go on.

I shall finish in a few minutes. In order to get some degree of balance in the economy of this country, if Canada is to become a nation, it will be necessary for the federal government to do some planning itself. So far as I can see, unless the federal government is prepared to institute a programme of public investment in the maritime provinces by way of secondary industries, there is no solution for the problem; it will become worse and worse as the years go by.
I notice that the provincial government has a capital budget this year, and it is spending some money, a little on the highways and on hospitals, and on hotel extension.
What do you call a little?

Not much; an odd million or half a million here and there. But the point I make is this, that while these expenditures are all desirable, none of them is a wealth-producing project. They will take the edge off for a short time by some construction work, and will result in hiring some labour at thirty cents an hour to work on the highways, as usual. But some secondary industries must be put into that part of the country.
We have tried it. For example, a small canning factory attempted to open up in Sydney, but they have been held up for about seven months on a molasses quota; and they are still held up. The bridging of the strait of Canso would have got us through this transition period, so far as unemployment is concerned; and that was recommended to the house by a committee of the house in 1942. Nothing has yet been done about it. The borings are completed; the cost of the project is known. In a return tabled in the house on April 23 the Minister of Transport (Mr. The Budget-Mr. Gillis

Chevrier) definitely stated that a causeway across the strait of Canso would cost $17,797,000; a bridge, $27,276,000. He ended by saying that this project could not be started because the policy had not been determined. They have been determining that since 1942. That project would have employed 4,000 men for a period of three years and would have got us through this difficult period.
May I ask the hon. member who quotes $26 million?

That is an estimate from the Department of Transport, contained in a return brought down in answer to a question by the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black). In 1946 an appropriation of $300,000 was voted for the building of a breakwater on Cape Breton island. Although the money was appropriated, nothing has so far been done. That would have created considerable employment. A fish processing plant and a big freezing plant are held up on the island of Cape Breton because the necessary repairs to a wharf in the Point Edward area along the Waterford coastline is held up. Those necessary establishments are held up because the necessary repairs have not been made to a wharf. Many things could be done down there.
I should like to conclude my remarks by saying that if the government is saving its public works programme to take the country over a difficult period which may come two years from now-I will not say for election purposes-they are making a mistake. Quite a few hon. members on the other side of the house who know something about the system and about economics realize that there will be a recession within the next couple of years. It may be a good thing to save the public works programme in Ontario and Quebec and other provinces where there is no recession, but in the maritime provinces the time to commence public works programmes was a year ago. The public works projects to which I have referred are national assets, because, if they are not carried out, when the government gets around to creating some employment in Nova Scotia there will be nobody there to work, since they are leaving that province every day. Our best people are leaving. In the maritimes we lose fifteen thousand a year to the United States. The people who were employed are pulling out.
I would seriously suggest that subsidies, which dovetail into the budget, should again be paid. The removal of the subsidies is the thing which will prevent us from holding the price line and everything else. I do not think it can be held without subsidies.
[Mr. Gillis.7
The minister said that he had a large surplus. That is fine, if the function of the government is to save money and produce large surpluses and allow certain sections of the country to go to pieces, but I do not think it is good government. If the minister had taken some of the millions of dollars which he boasted about here a few nights ago; if he had taken $5 million of that surplus and given it to the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) in February, we would not have had the whole economy of Nova Scotia torn to pieces today because of a strike in the coal industry, which is the basis of the whole economy of that province. I seriously suggest that the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Labour have a conference to see if the Minister of Labour cannot wheedle a subsidy out of the Minister of Finance in order to break the deadlock down there and get something done.

Mr. Speaker, I fail to see, for the Canadian people, any occasion for excessive rejoicings in the advent of a new minister in the Department of Finance. Although no doubt can be entertained as to the ability of both the present minister (Mr. Abbott) and his predecessor, it nevertheless remains apparent to all who listen to them or bow to their wishes, that both these men are equally intent on emptying, as far as possible, the pockets of the Canadian taxpayers.
"The country", states the horn, the Minister of Finance, "enjoys a degree of prosperity unknown in our generation." Without fear of contradiction' one might also add that it enjoys the very doubtful privilege of having the most extensive black market organization ever, that the people are still at the beck and call of the most powerful and costliest bureaucracy of our history, that they experience the most terrible scarcity of building materials ever known and that hundreds of Canadians wear themselves out hunting for non-existent housing accommodation, that the burden of taxation is the heaviest ever born by our people in peace time, that the gross debt of Canada is at its peak, since, on March 31, 1947 it had reached a total of $17,659,627,000, while it stood at $3,540,237,614, on March 31, 1938.
The government has announced a surplus of $352,000,000 for the fiscal year just ended, but it should not be forgotten that in addition to the revenue derived from the liberal War Assets Corporation, Canadians, during the fiscal year 1946-47, paid $16,340,000 in excise

The Budget-Mr. Gagnon
taxes on automobiles compared to $6,701,000 in 1945-46, which represents an increase of $9,639,000.
On cigars, cigarettes and tobacco, they paid $76,318,000 as against $70,229,000 in 1945-46, the increase amounting to $6,089,000.
On cigarette paper and tubes, $6,943,000 as against $4,645,000 in 1945-46, which represents an increase of $2,298,000.
On gasoline, car owners paid $36,220,000, compared with $29,836,000 in 1945-46, the increase amounting to $6,384,000.
On phonographs, radios and tubes, $2,526,000 as against $646,000 in 1945-46, the increase amounting to $1,880,000.
In 1946-47, Canadians paid $1,185,000 on imports but only $787,000 in 1945-46, which represents an increase of $398,000.
On sugar, $11,339,000 in 1946-47 as against $9,974,000 in 1945-46, which represents an increase of $1,365,000.
On amusements, $14,552,000 in 1946-47 as against $13,387,000 in 1945-46, representing an increase of $1,165,000.
On non-alcoholic beverages, they paid $18,634,000 as against $16,657,000 in 1945-46, the increase amounting to $1,977,000.
In other words, Canadian taxpayers paid a total of $1,022,120,000 in indirect taxes, as against $821,485,000 in 1945-46, which represents an increase of $200,635,000.
After paying $1,436,400,000 in direct taxes, including $695,000,000 in the form of personal income tax, I am of the opinion that the taxpayers really deserved more than the slight income tax reductions provided for in the budget. The Minister of Finance should have thanked the Canadian people for its magnificent financial support and modestly conceded that the Government had been free to spend as it wished the money thus obtained.
I also find the Minister of Finance rather presuming in his praise of the "speed and smoothness with which we have made the transition from war to peace."
In the opinion of many people, this transition is on the contrary quite difficult and even more costly than the one which followed the first world war. The last two wars in which we have been forced to participate have left painful memories in our minds, and have deeply affected both our hearts and our pocketbooks. People have not forgotten that from 1915 to 1944 they gave away to the federal government, in war taxes and succession duties alone, a total of $9,476,158,656. They are hoping for a 'breathing spell. The workers who toiled and moiled from 1939 to 1947 to fill the sieve-like coffers of the dominion treasury feel perfectly justified in asking leave to think of themselves and their families. Too much of their war-time wages has been swallowed up by Ottawa for them to put money aside, while this year's budget holds the promise of a future that is anything but rosy. A substantial reduction in tax rates, especially on personal incomes, is necessary if the government wish to avoid criticism on the part of poor people and small wage-earners, if they sincerely desire to prevent the spread of subversive ideas and if they intend to leave to the worker the fruits of his labour so that he may face the future with some confidence. Let us provide our people with bread, clothing and houses and they, in turn, will show their gratitude to their leaders by their respect of the laws and their disregard for diabolical suggestions put forward by communist or other agitators. Such is the request which I place before the authorities on behalf of the fine constituency of Chicoutimi which I have the honour to represent in this house.
I thank the' hon. Minister of Finance for his statement that the government of which he is a member "do not contemplate a continuing, large-scale programme of government lending to finance our exports." It is gratifying to hear that the gifts to England have ended and that our government have now decided to look after the affairs of our own country.
Then, he will perhaps find time to solve the problem of dominion-provincial relations, about which I hope I may be allowed to say a few words.
On April 2, 1947, the Montreal chamber of commerce, whose 4,300 members are business men of that city, unanimously passed an important brief on dominion-provincial relations.
Since the problem is weighty and the group which has tackled it extremely competent, the brief deserves the attention of our present leaders and I believe all who are interested in seeing happy relations between the dominion and the provinces would be well advised to consider it.
After openly heralding the importance of "fully preserving all constitutional guarantees granted the provinces," the chamber of commerce stated that:
. . . the present dominion proposals would bring about too great an economic and financial centralization.
It adds that the principle on which these proposals are based invariably suggests that the provinces surrender, in return for financial compensation, their power to tax incomes, profits and estates.
The Budget-Mr. Gagnon

The very definition of that procedure evidently implies at least partial centralization as regards not only the levying of tax, but also the enacting of tax legislation. Because of this latter implication, such procedure impedes the free exercise of the rights granted the provinces by the constitution. Provincial autonomy in the taxation field does not consist only in the collection of revenue now purported to be sufficient; a government which is deprived of its power to levy taxes is no longer a true government, because its action is dependent upon that of the authority holding the power of the purse.
After warning against the danger of subsidies which inevitably lead to bargaining between the dominion and the provinces, the memorandum continues as follows:
Much stress is laid on the fact that the agreements would be of a temporary nature, thus preserving the autonomy of the provinces, which could recover at the end of the five-year period, the rights yielded to the dominion government. This argument is in itself sufficient proof that they would have to abandon temporarily the rights and privileges conferred by their autonomy.
As 'the reasons given to justify such relinquishment are of a permanent nature (maintenance of prosperity through a centralized cyclical budget, through a centralized policy of social security and full employment), it is difficult to see how the nominal five-year period provided for in the proposed agreements could really be significant. Such agreements do not contain any automatic resolutory clause; therefore it would be necessary for the dissatisfied provinces to denounce them in order theoretically to put an end to their operation after the expiration of the basic period. Any province which is not ready to relinquish definitely its taxing power in the fields covered by such agreements must, if it is conscious of its responsibilities to its cititzens and to the country, refrain from authorizing the dominion to put into operation a comprehensive and permanent economic control 'and social security programme if, in order to retain its constitutional rights it must, five years hence, withdraw from the programme and thus disrupt this machinery. In other words, the settlement of permanent problems, such as full employment and social security by means of temporary agreements could give rise to serious political strife at a time when the country would be in the greatest need of the loyal cooperation of every party.
Finally, in their belief that "agreements between Ottawa and the provinces are needed to maintain in this country the atmosphere of security which is essential to its progress" the Chamber of Commerce submits as a basis for a common understanding that-
(a)	each government retain the right to initiate legislation in the fields of taxation allotted to it under the constitution, which seems to be the only system consistent with their respective autonomies;
(b)	the provincial governments being restricted to direct taxation, they should be free to resort to it according to their needs;

(c)	all governments agree to simplify the tax collection system and to exchange all information needed for such a simplification and for the standardization of legislation.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the Montreal Chamber of Commerce is to be commended. It has proved equal to the fine reputation which it has gained throughout Canada in the past. Coming as it does in the wake of the Quebec premier's statement, his brief clearly shows that the people of this country are of one mind on this vital matter and that representations made on their behalf by the provincial authorities truly reflect their outlook and aspirations.
My last point is about the Canadian National Railways, whose deficit of over nine and a half millions we've had to make good this year. Should not the government be well advised to consider the possibility of refinancing our railway system's consolidated indebtedness through a new government-hacked bond issue at only 2 per cent? With the present rate of between 3 and 5 per cent, in 1946 alone the Canadian public have had to foot an interest bill of $23,358,514.18 on a debt of $530,422,997.55. At 2 per cent, they wouldn't have to pay more than $10,608,459.95.
The saving thus achieved, namely $12,750,054.23, might we'll be used to improve the service between Montreal, Quebec City and Chicoutimi, so that our district might at long last receive the decent and fair treatment it deserves. The government would do well to give this matter special attention and, they will earn the gratitude of the people of Canada, especially those in the county of Chicoutimi, if the necessary steps are taken.

If I had been sure that
the estimates of the Department of Agriculture would be taken up in the not too distant future, Mr. Speaker, I might have refrained from speaking on this occasion. However I deem it expedient to come back to this question which to such a great degree interests the potato growers of New Brunswick. On February 4, I covered the problem in a general manner and pointed out that it is in bumper crop years that prices go down below the cost of production. I also pointed out that, in the opinion of the farmers of New Brunswick, something should be done to ensure reasonable marketing at all times. In furtherance of that objective I expressed the view that an adequate price could be obtained only through some sort of orderly marketing under an agency of the government. As far as Ii know, that was the first time that such a policy had been advocated in the house. I was not sure

The Budget-Mr. Michaud
then that the idea would meet with universal approval. It would be presumptuous on my part to claim that it did meet with universal approval, but I can stay that all those who wrote to me or spoke to me about it-and there were many who did'-agreed entirely with the suggestions I made on that occasion. In any event, nobody expresed disagreement with the plan suggested, and for that reason I feel that it meets with practically universal approval on the part of our growers.
Before turning to what I feel should be done as regards the future, may I say a word as to what has happened since I spoke in the house on February 4. As hon. members know, shortly after that date the United Kingdom placed an order for a considerable quantity of table stock potatoes from Prince Edward Island, something which probably never happened before and is not likely to occur in the future. Then we received orders from Portugal and Brazil, which was also something unheard of as regards table stock potatoes. In the meantime it turned out that the United States found out to their sorrow that they were short of potatoes with which to fill orders they had accepted from European countries. We all know that early last winter the Lnited States government destroyed considerable quantities of potatoes because, at that time, they had no hope of finding a market for them. But somehow or another they carried the dumping of potatoes too far in the state of Maine. This is the only reason why the price of potatoes rose around April 20. In other words, it was the blunder of the United States government which brought some measure of relief to our farmers recently and at the same time saved this government from the serious embarrassment of having to go into the potato business on May 1, pursuant to the order in council passed last October. In my opinion, this is nothing short of miraculous and it is not likely to happen another year.
The fact that the government was miraculously saved from serious embarrassment as a result of improvident action in the United States should not prevent us from facing the problem for the future as it should be faced. The wheat growers of the west have their Canadian Wheat Board Act which guarantees them a floor price for their product. There is an effective minimum or floor price for practically all farm products. Potatoes are the only exception. The result is that we are left to struggle with the implacable law of supply and demand, which is neither fair nor equitable in years such as 1946. We are also exposed to, and are often victims of, unfair competition in marketing.
In the winter of 1945, when I sat in the legislature of New Brunswick, I heard it said time and again that unfair marketing practices were being carried on in New Brunswick particularly as regards the marketing of seed potatoes in South and Central America. An order would come up and a certain price would be arrived at between the dealers. Then another dealer would underbid the former and get the order. It would appear that such unfortunate practices occurred again during the present crop year. It is commonly stated, and not denied, that on the Saint John river, as a result of such unfair competition, the farmers lost money to the tune of some 135,000 in connection with the sale to Argentina last fall.
That is peanuts.

It may be peanuts to the hon. member for Springfield, but it is not peanuts to the average farmer in my constituency and it possibly is not peanuts to the average farmer in his own constituency. The farmers are again under the impression that something similar occurred recently in connection with the orders from Portugal. Whether there is any truth in the rumour or not is of no practical consequence now, because prices have gone up above anything that the farmers could possibly get on those orders from Portugal and Brazil.
I bring out those facts in order to illustrate the necessity of an effective marketing agency for our farmers. The farmers do ask for such an agency. In support of their request, may I quote from certain reports published in divers papers at the time of the farmers' convention or meeting here in Ottawa sometime around the end of February. The first one is from the Ottawa Journal of February 27, and reads in part as follows:
The meeting, called by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture requested the directors of the federation to place before the government a draft federal agricultural products marketing act to be dealt with at the present session of parliament.
And further down:
The proposed act would set up a dominion marketing board with control over distribution, quantity, quality, variety and maximum and minimum prices of regulated farm products in interprovincial and export markets.
And further down:
G. F. Perkin. Ontario government director of marketing, told the delegates "practically all" cash crops in his province were under marketing schemes, but many farmers felt the need of extending regulations to cover interprovincial and export trade.
The Budget-Mr. Michaud

When the large majority of producers of a particular product agreed on a marketing plan for their crops, it was "a question of fairness or common justice ' that the plan should apply to all.
In the Telegraph-Journal, a New Brunswick newspaper, of February 28, we find a report of the meeting, from which I want to quote just one paragraph:
The federation would have the government set up a dominion marketing board with powers to regulate, distribution, grades, quantity, prices and marketing of certain farm goods going from one province to another or into foreign trade.
Again in the Telegraph-Journal of March 3 I read the report of a meeting of farmers held at Bristol, which I think is in the county of Carleton:
A well attended meeting of potato growers and shippers was held in the community hall at Bristol. Mr. . . . was named chairman and Mr. . . . secretary.
I skip part of it and come to the material paragraph:
It was decided that it was advisable at this time to send a delegation to Ottawa. Setting up of a marketing board and steps to bring about acreage control were discussed. A committee of five was set up to meet the New Brunswick potato council to discuss various matters.
The meeting went on record as being unanimously behind any organization set-up to assist the growers obtain a fair price for potatoes.
There does not seem to be any doubt that our farmers want efficient marketing agencies for their products. Our next consideration is, which government has jurisdiction in the matter? I am well aware of the fact that on this question of marketing we touch upon a complicated constitutional problem. I hardly know more than the ABC's of constitutional law, but the experts of the Department of Justice will be able to correct me if I go too far astray. For that reason I venture to express the following views on the constitutional aspects of the problem. In the first place, I feel that the matter of controlled acreage is strictly one within provincial jurisdiction. The question of marketing, however, may be a matter of either provincial or federal jurisdiction according to the extent of the trade involved. Under section 91 (2) of the British North America Act the federal government has jurisdiction with regard to the regulation of trade and commerce. This section of the act has come up for interpretation in a number of cases, most of which went to the privy council. I have carefully reviewed the digests of the cases, and have come to the conclusion that the gist of the decisions is that the provinces have jurisdiction to regulate trade and commerce within their 
own boundaries but have no authority or jurisdiction to regulate foreign and interprovincial trade.
It is probably due to that generally accepted interpretation that the province of New Brunswick in its act of 1937 respecting the control of agricultural products purported to give to its board authority to-
-fix from time to time, the price or prices, maximum price or prices, minimum price or prices, at which natural products may be sold in the province at wholesale for resale or use in the province.
That is section 4(1) (c) of our provincial act. Under this act the province cannot fix prices on agricultural products going out of the province. I presume the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) has good reasons for not introducing during the course of the present session a farm products marketing act in accordance with the representations of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. The need for this legislation may not be so urgent in regard to farm products other than potatoes. It is true that under our export and import permits legislation, which was passed early this session, it might be possible to regulate to some extent the export of our potatoes to foreign countries, but in my opinion this would be a clumsy and unsatisfactory manner of trying to regulate this important part of our external trade. Potatoes are one of our important cash crops, possibly the second largest export cash crop, though I have not the figures to make that statement without reservation. In any event, it is of considerable importance, and for that reason I feel that something should be done to ensure proper export marketing.
Then there is the matter of interprovincial trade. New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island supply a considerable quantity of the potatoes consumed in other provinces, particularly in Quebec and Ontario. Marketing in these provinces has never been satisfactory because of the lack of proper marketing organizations. For those reasons I feel that we should have a potato marketing board1 immediately, quite independent of any agricultural products act which may be set up at some future time. May I point out to the Minister of Agriculture that the provincial minister of agriculture agrees with me in this matter. In order that there may be no misunderstanding about it, I wish to quote from a letter from him dated April 22, 1947. Mr. Taylor, who by the way is possibly the most competent minister of agriculture we have had in New Brunswick since confederation, writes in part as follows:
I am definitely of the opinion that a central marketing agency is the only means by which

The Budget-Mr. Michaud
New Brunswick potatoes can be marketed to the satisfaction of all concerned. I have stressed this in no uncertain terms with the growers, the dealers and the federal authorities.
Then he refers to our New Brunswick act:
This act is largely along similar lines to that which is in effect in a great many of the provinces, but acts of this nature have no authority in regard to controlling the marketing of any product in export or interprovincial movement. A marketing plan was set up under this act but due to its being general knowledge that there was no legislative power dealing with the export it was of no effect. I have strongly urged on the federal authorities that in order to make provincial marketing legislation effective it is necessary to have a federal act that has the authority in regard to interprovineial and export movements.
And further down:
I trust that the present legislation which is being considered in Ottawa will give the federal authority that is necessary to make a complete job of the necessary legislative authority and should that be the case we would be only too glad to urge on the producers in New Brunswick to organize in order that they may take advantage of same, but failing to provide federal legislation it is absolutely out of the question for our growers to organize and control the marketing under our provincial legislation.
Mr. F. W. Squires, a member of the New Brunswick legislature and former leader of the opposition, recently referred to this matter, I believe in the month of April although I have not the exact date. As reported in the Telegraph-Journal he had this to say:
I must say, however, that as regards the expansion of our potato industry, that the minister of agriculturefie is referring to the provincial minister. -has done the best he could, but has met with a refusal to cooperate from certain interests and by a cold-blooded and refractory attitude by the dominion government.
I know those remarks are not justified in so far as they relate to the federal government, but I just wanted to point out to the minister the form of criticism which is likely to materialize in New Brunswick if something is not done by this government to bring about a better marketing of our huge crop of potatoes. I urge the minister either to introduce legislation during the present session or to give such assurance regarding marketing as may be necessary to put our farmers at rest in connection with this problem which is so vital to them. I want to emphasize the importance of their having something definite in this connection before seeding gets underway in my province, and that is the reason I am speaking tonight.
If we are to rely entirely on the Agricultural Prices Support Act should our 1947 crop turn out to be as heavy as the 1946 crop, what
will be the policy of the board in assisting the farmers? I wish to warn the minister that, although the steps taken last fall were sound and he is to be commended for taking them, any purchasing which may be done by the government in order to relieve a situation similar to the one we had this winter will have to be done before May 1, and even before April 1, if it is to be of any real assistance to the farmer. The peak price for potatoes is reached about March 1, and I submit that any future policy similar to the one adopted last year should provide for a date not later than March 1. How the date of May 1 was arrived at last fall I do not know, but there has been considerable criticism along the Saint John river as to what occurred when a high official of this Department of Agriculture went there. I do not wish to air that criticism on the floor of the house, but if the minister wishes I shall be glad to tell him confidentially what the farmers are complaining about, and, in my opinion, rightly so.
The easiest and the wisest way to overcome all this difficulty is to provide marketing legislation during the present session. I submit that a potato marketing board could be operated with a minimum of cost to the government and a maximum of efficiency for our farmers. I know some hon. members will say that this is socialistic legislation. Personally I do not care very much about words and definitions; what I am interested in is results. After all, it is hardly conceivable to have a state 100 per cent socialistic or 100 per cent private enterprise. The business of any government should be to strike a happy medium between those two extreme views. We have already nationalized a number of the utilities and services in this country, and with good results. In any event, this marketing board would not be any more socalistic than the wheat board and the other boards which, in my opinion, are performing useful functions. Before leaving this point I wish to urge the minister once more to tell our farmers what they may depend upon next year in the nature of assistance against the possibility of a situation similar to that which prevailed until a few weeks ago in New Brunswick.
Before resuming my seat I wish to make a few comments on some of the criticisms which were voiced by some of the members of the opposition. As we say in French, "A tout seigneur tout honneur". I shall begin with the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario (Mr. Macdonnell). In his able speech he used the word "disappointment" very often. To those of us who were sitting on this side
The Budget-Mr. Michaud

of the house it was easy to read disappointment on the faces of the Conservative members when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) announced the reduction in personal income taxes. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) previously had advocated a cut of thirty per cent. He made sure that the target was too high to be reached by the Minister of Finance, but when it turned out that the average reduction was twenty-nine per cent our hon. friends opposite were very much disappointed and their disappointment was evident on their faces.
The hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario referred, with tears in his eyes, to the middle class which was not being properly looked after, and he defined that middle class as those with incomes between $3,000 and $7,500. What should be understood by the term "middle class" is not easy to determine. One might think it referred to the middle third of our population from the income point of view, and a more liberal interpretation might take in a larger proportion, possibly the fifty per cent of the middle group between the lower and the higher income brackets. But no matter how we look at it, I cannot agree with the hon. member as to where this middle class should fit in to the scale of income earners.
During the 1946 session the hon. member for Lethbridge (Mr. Blackmore) placed on Hansard a letter received from the bureau of statistics over the signature of Mr. J. L. Forsyth, statistician. From this letter it appears that according to the 1941 census 32-9 of all wage-earners in Canada had an income of less than $450 a year-that is for the year from June 1, 1940 to June 1, 1941- 31-6 per cent had an income of less than $950; 91-5 per cent had an income of less than $1,950, and there were only 6-8 per cent in receipt of incomes over $1,950 a year. Assuming that those figures would require revision upwards in order to bring them in line with present-day wages, I think it is fair to assume that possibly today 75 per cent instead of 91-5 per cent, as in 1941, do not earn more than $2,000.
If we look at the problem from the point of view of income tax returns filed for the year 1945 we find that there are only 165,000 taxpayers with incomes between $3,000 and $7,500, which is much less than seven per cent of the total number of income taxpayers and is only 1-4 per cent of the total population of Canada. In addition, there are 34,500 income taxpayers paying on incomes of $7,500 or more. If we take all taxpayers with net incomes of $3,000 or more we find that they represent about eight per cent of the total taxpayers, and only about 1-7 per cent

of the total population. I submit that those figures establish conclusively that the middle class referred to by the financial critic of the opposition cannot, by any stretch of the imagination, be considered as a truly middle class of our population. It may be said at the most that it constitutes the middle class of the top five or six per cent in the upper income brackets. As I look at those figures I come to the conclusion that what I consider our middle class is practically income tax exempt, at least so far as married people are concerned, and it is with those people that the government should be primarily concerned.
The hon. gentleman mentioned that much of our foreign trade is made possible only by the fact that we lend money. According to an answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), and, I think, filed during the present session, it appears that our exports for 1946 amounted roughly to $2,300 million as against $1,900 million for our imports, leaving a favourable trade balance of some $400 million.
Our loans to Great Britain and to other European countries amounted to something in the neighbourhood of $2 billion, of which $648 million were used up in 1946. The loan clearly contemplated-and no one knows this better than the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario-and may I say I am sorry he is not in his seat-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: He is ill, as a matter of fact.

The loan contemplated that, to the extent and for the duration of the loan period, we should carry out this loan to a very large extent by our excess of exports over our imports. How could it be done otherwise? Would the hon. gentleman find it better business if our imports had balanced evenly with our exports, with the result that we should have had to advance in actual cash the whole sum of $648 million instead of approximately $264 million, as we actually did.
If we subtract from our total exports that portion which was made possible through lending, there are still left exports to the extent of $1,700 million, which is approximately twice our pre-war exports, and even higher than our wartime exports prior to 1942. When we bear this in mind it will be recognized that Canada is not doing too badly in the matter of foreign trade. And for that reason I cannot see any object in the remarks to which I have just referred, to the effect that our foreign trade is possible only by the fact that we lend money. When the

The Budget-Mr. Michaud
financial critic of the opposition has to refer to this type of criticism, it strikes me that their party cannot find much that is seriously wrong with the budget.
There is just one other subject of criticism from the same hon. gentleman, which struck me most forcibly. It is his reference to the easy money policy of this government and the question of interest rates.
At page 2803 of Hansard we find the following remarks:
For that reason I say that I believe the preservation of a strong middle class-
Again the middle class.
-is important not merely economically but as going down to the very roots of our political being.
And further down:
Fifty years ago the man who retired with a modest competency could get five or six per cent on it and he could reckon on living the rest of his life upon the proceeds. What happens today when he receives three per cent? And he is lucky if he gets that.
And further down:
I suggest that this very important factor be taken into consideration-it is very important indeed-that there are large elements in the community who are suffering greatly by that policy. One other thing I would like to say in that connection. I would ask whether we can go on freeing other things and leaving the rate of interest tied down tight.
Mr. Speaker, this is where I and, I hope, the vast majority of Liberal members in the house-I am sure my hon. friends directly opposite share this view-and, I hope, the great majority of the people of this country, say we differ radically from the policy of the Progressive Conservative party.
On the other hand, I am grateful that the party has so clearly expounded its position on this important question. The hon. member fears that interest rates will remain tied down tight, I regret to say that his fears fill me with joy. Yes; I do hope that interest rates will remain tied down and will be pressed further down, and tighter. In the middle ages theologians and moralists took the view that it was sinful to charge interest on money lent. This practice was generally described as usury. The immortal drama by Shakespeare, "The Merchant of Venice", is based almost entirely on this very principle. For some reason or another the churches relaxed from this hard and fast rule, and gave tacit approval to the charging of interest, I suppose the answer of the moralist to this change of attitude as regards the ethics of charging interest might be explained in terms somewhat similar to those of the Divine Teacher when asked why, under the old law, a man was permitted to have more than one wife. When it comes to
quoting scripture, I am not well versed, and I would not know where to find the passage in question. But my recollection is that the answer was somewhat along this line, that it was on account of the hardness of their hearts. Possibly it was on account of the hardness of the hearts of moneylenders that interest rates were subsequently tacitly approved by moralists and theologians.
Why should anyone be reaping interest, clipping coupons on gilt-edged securities, and sit idle, while someone else toils to pay the interest on those bonds? Why should anyone thrive, in that manner, on the fat of the land? Our present-day civilization, with its highly developed economic and financial system, makes it possible for a person to set aside for the future the proceeds of his labour, in excess of his immediate wants. This excess of his productive activity he can convert into money or liquid assets, and tuck it away in absolute safety to be used at some future time. This happy state of affairs was hardly possible centuries ago, and it is not likely possible in countries which have not reached our degree of civilization, as, for instance, great portions of Asia and Africa.
But the fact that our society makes this situation possible should be sufficient reward for the saver. Therefore there should be no necessity for paying him, in addition, juicy interest in the nature of additional reward for his savings. Please bear in mind that in speaking about interest in this vein I have in mind gilt-edged securities, such as government bonds, and so on. There are a great many people in this country who think as I do. May I just refer to one of them for the time being. Every member in the house knows, or should know, about Wilfred C. Krug, who, every once in a while, writes open letters and advises the Minister of Finance and parliament how to handle money situations. I had heard of this gentleman some time before coming to this house, and I agreed with him almost entirely on financial matters. For that reason I save every letter that comes from him, and commend his writings to the attention of all those who are eager to listen to the other side of the story. Much as I should like to quote extensively from Mr. Krug, I shall confine myself to just two paragraphs which appeared in a letter reproduced in the Windsor Daily Star of March 26, 1947:
While we detest the reparation policy that Russia is trying to impose on conquered countries, -we completely overlook the burden that was imposed upon the Canadian people as a result of the war. A sum of $481,207,000 annually is being exacted from the Canadian people in the form of interest on the national debt, It is a form of reparation demanded by s creditor class for loaning money to help win the
The Budget-Mr. Michaud

war. While those who stayed at home loaned their money at interest, one million Canadians offered their lives without interest. This creditor class will receive approximately $10,000 million interest (reparation) during the coming twenty years and the debt will still remain unpaid. The class will profit year after year because of war. "The burden will continue to be onerous not only for us but for the next two or three generations" unless we do something sensible about the matter.
While we condemn Russia for the violation of the rights of people in other countries, it behooves us to make sure that the rights of our own Canadians are observed here in Canada. These rights are not observed when the Canadian people are taxed $481,207,000 annually in order to permit a creditor class to profit year after year from war. By refunding the national debt, as it matures, through the Bank of Canada, we can get rid of the interest burden. The Bank of Canada has been used to finance $1,868,000,000 of the national debt. It can be used to finance the remaining $15,000 million as well.
I know the hon. member for Muskoka-Ontario and most of his colleagues would not be able to subscribe to the views of Mr. Krug. I am particularly glad, however, that the Conservative party has placed itself on record in no uncertain terms on this much debated question of interest rates.
Are you placing the Liberals on record?

I am placing my views on record. If there were any doubt as to whether the Conservatives had receded to some extent from their former position as defenders of big interests and special privileges this doubt has now been completely dispelled by the speech of the financial critic of their party, and for this fact I think we should all be duly grateful.
Just one more word on this point, and it is to urge the government to use the Bank of Canada to finance our national lending as suggested by Mr. Krug. If, however, they should be unable to subscribe wholly to this view I suggest then that everything be done to bring it about slowly by reducing interest rates gradually so that eventually the same results can be achieved. In my opinion there is only one justification for interest being charged, and it is in cases where some degree of risk is involved. If I borrow money to go into business-the lender is perfectly justified in charging me interest at a rate commensurate with the risk involved, but where there is no risk, as in government bonds, I fail entirely to see the reason for the payment of interest, at least at more than a nominal rate. I think my time has expired. Much as I should like to continue I shall conclude.

This budget reminds me somewhat of the weather; very few people like it; everybody talks about 
it, and the only one who can do anything about it does not seem to want to. However, speaking in support of the subamendment moved by my leader, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell), I desire to use most of my time in dealing with the budget and its effects on the farmers of this country. But before doing so, may I make a few observations of a general nature?
First, I wish to repeat what I have said on many previous occasions, that the first charge on the production of a nation must be a decent standard of living for those people who make that production possible. A corollary to that is the fact that a nation's greatness is judged by how well it provides for the aged, the sick, and those suffering from physical handicaps. This was so ably presented by my colleagues, the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) and the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Thatcher), that I need not enlarge on it. But I wish to underline their questions wherein they asked why this government is so reluctant to establish the social security programme outlined prior to the dominion-provincial conferences; I would even go farther and add, at least with those provinces that have shown their willingness to cooperate by signing an agreement.
While we all enjoyed the able speech delivered by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), yet it was astounding to many of us that a man in such a responsible position could adopt such an air of easy indifference to the-needs of so many people. For example, he said, as reported on page 2554 of Hansard:
The exemption levels established last year are high enough to exempt completely from tax more than half the people earning incomes in, Canada. Consequently it can be said that any person who pays income tax now has more than an average income, taking his or her marital and dependent status into account.
As my leader so ably proved in his statement which appears on page 2809 of Hansard, the present exemptions are below bare living requirements. Is any greater indictment needed of our present financial and economic system than that, in the peak years of national production and income, over half of our people earning incomes should be forced to exist on substandard levels? But our Minister of Finance blandly goes on in the style of a barker for Ringling Brothers. A person could almost hear him say, "Hurry, hurry, hurry; come this way and see the biggest freak of the year." Just listen to what he said on page 2554 of Hansard:
I am consequently proposing to make a substantial reduction in taxation in this budget. Moreover I am proposing to concentrate this reduction almost entirely in the field of personal income tax.

The Budget-Mr. Burton
If the general public fall for that kind of shell game, then P. T. Barnum's famous words are true. The minister said that he was proposing to concentrate the reduction in taxation almost entirely in the field of personal income tax, while conveniently obscuring the fact that he was piling another $10 million reduction on the $279 million melon that big business had presented to them in the previous budget. In addition to this, the excess profits tax will disappear entirely before this fiscal year is over, which, in the ultimate end;, means that the personal income taxpayer is at the short end of the bargain.
When we look at the table on page 2552 of Hansard we find that the Minister of Finance expects a revenue of $325 million from the sales tax, which is an increase of $27 million above last year. It must be borne in mind, as has been pointed out on previous .occasions, that the sales tax bears most heavily on those who can least afford it, and should have been reduced or entirely eliminated from everything except those articles which are out-and-out luxuries. But in his hurry to eliminate the excess profits tax the minister could not see his way clear to do so. He even turned a deaf ear to the kiddies in their plea, and continues to filch pennies from them when they buy their pop and candies. Here is another gem from the minister's speech at page 2559 of Hansard:
A short time ago in this house I urged Canadian business men to reduce their prices as their volume and efficiency of business expand. I stated that it is neither proper nor even good business to charge all the traffic will bear. I *want to emphasize that view again now. We in the government, and the vast majority in this house and in this country-
I believe he took in too much territory there, I may interject.
-believe in what is now called "free enterprise." We believe in it not as a windy doctrine or a mystic ideology, but as a sensible way of getting things done.
I will prove to him before I am through what that is worth.
It must prove itself and justify itself by its results. With the orderly removal of controls, with increasing supplies of material, with efficient and cooperative labour-
He does not want much, does he?
-and with ample markets, Canadian business enterprise is in a most favourable situation. We all expect it to show its mettle both in production and in marketing. We expect it to show its ability to keep down costs and prices.
And how, I may interject.
In its own long-run interest, as well as in the national interest, business must keep its prices down and its profits within reason.
What a hope! Yes, what a hope! I have here a clipping from the Rural Co-operator entitled "Surprise":
It is only a year ago that the Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley, then Minister of Finance, solemnly told parliament that the wartime prices and trade board had assured itself that even with an increase of 12i per cent in implement prices the manufacturer would be earning for the ensuing year profits less than the average of 19,36-1939. It must have been la surprise, therefore, to Mr. Ilsley when he learned the other day that Massey-Harris Company Limited had, in 1946, at $2,125,569, its highest net profit since 1929.
Later on, the same paper says:
The one-hundredth anniversary of this company is therefore an occasion for rejoicing, although perhaps more so along Bay and King streets than out on Ontario farms. One index of the progress of Massey-Harris during 1946 was a net gain of four points in the listed value of the common stock. This meant a gain of thirty per cent on capital for anyone who shrewdly bought at the beginning of the year and sold at the end of the year-and, it should be borne in mind, such a gain would be untaxable income. Let a farmer buy a herd of purebred cattle at the beginning of the year and sell the same animals at the end of the year at thirty per cent gain-and he finds the profit on buying and selling that stock is taxable income.
The Rural Co-operator says further:
There would be more justice and wisdom in taxing the speculator's gain and exempting the farmer's.
I most heartily concur in that statement. This is not the only company that showed these profits. Just before I came to the chamber there was a slip on my desk referring to the Toronto Star of May 6, wherein it is said that an average increase of 54.9 per cent in net profits is revealed in the annual reports for 1946 of twenty-seven industrial companies. Again I say to the minister, what a hope !
We in this group and) most of the organized farmers agreed to the wheat agreement, believing that the government would hold the price line on the cost of living and production. But the government's action during past weeks caused many of us to believe that once again we have been betrayed, and this budget proves that suspicion. I wish that every farmer in the country could read the speech of the Minister of Finance and then read the one by my leader, the member for Rosetown-Biggar, because I am certain that at least eighty per cent of those farmers would vote for our subamendment wherein we express regret that the government failed to raise income tax exemptions and failed to make provision so as to enable more than half the population who are compelled to live on incomes below the present exemptions to have an opportunity to improve their standards of living.
